result.text: ChronoR addresses temporal link prediction on temporal knowledge graphs, a challenging problem due to non-stationary, heterogeneous data and complex temporal dependencies. Its key insight is to model relation- and time-conditioned interactions as k-dimensional rotations so that applying a learned rotation to a head-entity embedding moves it close to the corresponding tail embedding, thereby naturally encoding temporal and multi-relational dynamics. The method jointly learns dense embeddings for entities, relations, and time and parameterizes a rotation operator in high-dimensional space for each (relation, time) pair; training minimizes distance between rotated heads and tails so the model captures rich temporal–relational interactions and outperforms prior state-of-the-art methods on benchmark temporal KG link prediction tasks.

The paper tackles efficient, symmetry-preserving prediction of quantum Hamiltonian matrices for molecular systems, where maintaining SE(3) equivariance typically conflicts with computational and memory efficiency. The key insight is an architectural design that enforces SE(3)-equivariance while drastically reducing costly tensor-product operations and preventing exponential channel growth as atom types increase. The authors propose QHNet, an SE(3)-equivariant graph neural network that restructures equivariant message passing to cut tensor products by 92%, streamlines channels to limit dimensional blowup, and uses this lightweight equivariant circuitry to predict Hamiltonian entries. On four MD17 molecular datasets QHNet matches state-of-the-art accuracy with much faster runtimes and about 50% lower memory consumption.

The paper tackles the problem of choosing layerwise sparsity for magnitude-based neural network pruning, where prior work relies on heuristics or costly hyperparameter searches and performance depends critically on per-layer sparsity allocation. Their key insight is that pruning decisions should account for each layer’s contribution to the model-level ℓ2 distortion, so weight magnitudes can be rescaled into an importance score that reflects the global impact of removing parameters. They propose LAMP (layer-adaptive magnitude-based pruning), a simple, hyperparameter-free scoring scheme that rescales magnitudes by layer-level statistics to produce layerwise sparsities for global pruning, and show empirically on image classification tasks (including weight-rewinding setups) that LAMP consistently outperforms popular baselines. The method is lightweight to compute and requires no expensive tuning while yielding better sparsity–performance tradeoffs than existing layerwise allocation strategies.

The paper addresses the challenge of designing practical, high-performing active learning algorithms that work with deep neural networks by revisiting Fisher-information–based selection objectives. Its key insight is that bounds on maximum likelihood estimator (MLE) error expressed via the Fisher information can guide selection of informative batches, and that this classic criterion can be made tractable and efficient for neural models by exploiting linear-algebraic structure. The authors propose BAIT, an algorithm that selects batches by optimizing a Fisher-information–based bound on MLE error and implements this optimization with scalable matrix computations suited to modern hardware. Empirically, BAIT consistently outperforms prior active learning methods on both classification and regression tasks and is adaptable to different model architectures.

The paper tackles the problem of making neural architecture search (NAS) fast and broadly applicable to diverse, under-explored domains beyond computer vision, where AutoML could have the most impact. The key insight is that fixing a standard CNN topology but searching only over operation choices—specifically kernel sizes and dilations—gives rich multi-resolution feature extraction while dramatically reducing the search space, and that leveraging the Fourier diagonalization of convolution lets one efficiently compute mixtures of these operations. Building on this, the authors propose DASH, a differentiable NAS algorithm that uses Fourier-based diagonalization to perform weight-sharing over operation mixtures with improved asymptotic complexity, yielding up to 10× faster search in practice; they evaluate DASH on ten varied tasks (e.g., PDE solving, protein folding, heart disease detection) and show it outperforms state-of-the-art AutoML on most tasks while keeping search-plus-retraining overhead low (often under 2× the training time of a baseline CNN).

The paper addresses the slow and memory-intensive training of 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) for large-scale scene reconstruction and novel view synthesis. Its key insight is that scene decomposition combined with a distributed consensus optimization—specifically using ADMM—lets multiple local 3DGS models cooperate to learn a single high-quality global model while reducing per-node load and improving convergence stability. Methodologically, DOGS splits a scene into K spatial blocks, runs K local 3DGS trainings on slave nodes that periodically enforce consensus on shared Gaussian parameters with a global model on the master via ADMM, discards the local models after training, and uses only the global model for inference; this yields over 6× faster training on large scenes while maintaining or improving rendering quality.

The paper tackles the tension in offline reinforcement learning between conservatism—necessary to avoid overestimation under distribution shift—and robustness to observation deviations (e.g., sensor noise or adversarial perturbations), which excessive conservatism can undermine. The key insight is that introducing a conservative smoothing regularizer that enforces consistency and lowered value estimates not only at dataset states but also for nearby perturbed states can simultaneously preserve safety under distribution shift and improve robustness to observation errors. Methodologically, RORL augments standard offline RL by applying regularization on both the policy and value function for states in a neighborhood around dataset states, coupled with conservative value estimation for those neighborhoods; the authors provide tighter suboptimality bounds in linear MDPs and empirically show improved benchmark performance and resilience to adversarial observation perturbations.

The paper addresses the gap between state space models (SSMs) and Transformers for language modeling by targeting efficient long-range contextualization without sacrificing short-term representational power. Its key insight is that combining an SSM sublayer—which excels at capturing long-range dependencies with subquadratic complexity—with a block-wise Transformer sublayer—which handles local, short-term interactions—yields a hybrid that leverages the strengths of both families. The authors propose the Block-State Transformer (BST), present three fully parallelizable variants that integrate SSMs and block attention, and empirically show BST outperforms comparable Transformer architectures on language modeling perplexity, generalizes to longer sequences, and achieves over an order-of-magnitude layer-level speedup versus block-recurrent baselines under model parallelism.

The paper addresses communication bottlenecks in distributed/federated optimization by unifying two previously separate approaches for gradient compression—variance-reduced unbiased compressors (DIANA) and error-feedback for biased contractive compressors (EF21)—into a single framework that can handle both. The key insight is that compressors can be characterized by two parameters (bias and variance), and by designing an algorithm that exploits both error feedback and variance-reduction ideas one can recover DIANA and EF21 as special cases while enabling a broader class of compressors. The proposed method introduces a new algorithm (EF-BV) that operates with this generalized compressor class, combines independent randomness across workers with an error-correction mechanism, and leverages variance reduction to improve convergence as the number of workers grows. The authors prove linear convergence under suitable conditions, showing that EF-BV inherits the practical benefits of biased compressors like top-k and the theoretical scaling advantages of randomized unbiased schemes.

The paper tackles catastrophic overfitting in single-step adversarial training, a sudden collapse where models become vulnerable to multi-step attacks (PGD) despite appearing robust to single-step attacks (FGSM). The key insight is that using only maximal-perturbation single-step examples concentrates training on boundary points and ignores the continuum of adversarial directions, which distorts the decision boundary and creates a highly curved loss surface that single-step updates cannot reliably defend. The authors analyze this mechanism and propose a simple remedy—augmenting or modifying single-step training to include non-maximal or diversified adversarial examples (thereby sampling the adversarial direction more broadly) to regularize curvature and preserve robustness—showing this prevents catastrophic overfitting and enables single-step procedures to resist multi-step attacks.

result.text: The paper tackles link forecasting on temporal knowledge graphs, where existing embedding-based approaches often lack explainability and struggle with predicting future events while preserving temporal consistency. The key insight is that temporal logical rules—learned from temporal random walks—can capture interpretable, time-aware reasoning chains that generalize across datasets and support inductive transfer. The proposed method, TLogic, extracts weighted temporal rules from random walk patterns, uses them to rank candidate future links by aggregating rule evidence with time-consistent grounding, and demonstrates improved predictive performance and human-readable explanations on three benchmarks compared to state-of-the-art baselines.

The paper addresses how to build SE(3)-equivariant graph neural networks that balance expressiveness and computational efficiency for physics- and geometry-driven tasks. Its key insight is to introduce equivariant local complete frames—orthonormal bases constructed from node coordinates via cross products—that avoid direction degeneration and let tensor-valued features be projected into a compact, complete local representation. The method embeds these frames into graph neural network layers to process and combine projected tensor information efficiently (since frames are formed using only cross products), yielding an expressive yet computationally light SE(3)-equivariant architecture. Experiments on Newtonian dynamics and molecular conformation generation show the approach matches or outperforms prior equivariant models while being efficient.

The paper tackles improving neural network pruning beyond standard magnitude-based methods, which decide pruned weights solely by individual magnitude and can be short-sighted when multiple layers interact. The key insight is that magnitude pruning optimizes Frobenius-norm distortion only for a single layer, so extending this objective across multiple consecutive layers—i.e., looking ahead to how pruning in earlier layers affects downstream layers—yields better global fidelity. The authors propose "lookahead pruning," a simple algorithm that jointly selects weights to remove by minimizing multi-layer Frobenius distortion (effectively solving a small multi-layer optimization instead of independent per-layer thresholds) and demonstrate empirically that it consistently outperforms magnitude pruning on architectures like VGG and ResNet, especially at high sparsity.

The paper tackles the scalability and redundancy problems of batch active learning when very large batches are needed, where naive batch selection loses adaptivity and wastes labels on redundant examples. The key insight is that combining uncertainty scoring with an efficient diversity-aware selection procedure lets one retain the benefits of active learning while avoiding intra-batch redundancy even at batch sizes of 100K–1M. Methodologically, the authors propose a scalable sampling algorithm that ranks examples by uncertainty and then selects a diverse subset via fast approximate diversification (with implementation choices that make it computationally tractable at massive scale), empirically demonstrating large improvements over recent baselines and offering an initial theoretical label-complexity analysis for a related, approximately equivalent sampler.

The paper addresses the problem of selecting convolutional kernel sizes in CNNs—a hyperparameter that ideally should vary across layers and data but is expensive to search and poorly served by prior learnable-size approaches that use dilation and have limited descriptive bandwidth. The key insight is that one can learn continuous, high-bandwidth convolution kernels whose effective size is differentiable and adjustable during training without increasing parameter count, and that controlling kernel frequency content analytically avoids aliasing when scaling to larger effective receptive fields or higher-resolution inputs. The method, called FlexConv, parameterizes kernels in a continuous differentiable form (with a novel frequency-controllable parameterization) that lets the network learn kernel size and spectral properties end-to-end, enabling FlexNets that model long-range dependencies without pooling, generalize to larger resolutions, converge faster, and achieve strong performance on sequential and image benchmarks while outperforming prior learned-size and dilated-kernel approaches.

The paper tackles the scalability bottleneck of 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) training, which is typically restricted to a single GPU and thus cannot handle high-resolution or large-scale scenes; the key insight is that because each Gaussian only contributes to a small, dynamic subset of pixels, training can be distributed by communicating only the required Gaussians to the corresponding pixel partitions and dynamically balancing load. They implement this idea in Grendel, a distributed system that partitions 3DGS parameters across GPUs, uses sparse all-to-all communication to transfer relevant Gaussians to pixel shards, supports batched multi-view training (rather than one view at a time), and applies a simple sqrt(batch size) hyperparameter scaling rule. By enabling dynamic partitioning and sparse communication, Grendel scales 3DGS to tens of millions of Gaussians across many GPUs and demonstrably improves reconstruction quality on large, high-resolution scenes (e.g., raising PSNR from 26.28 to 27.28 on Rubble by moving from 11.2M Gaussians on one GPU to 40.4M on 16 GPUs).

The paper tackles the challenge of offline reinforcement learning where standard off-policy methods overestimate action values due to distributional shift between a static dataset and the learned policy, causing poor performance especially on complex, multi-modal data. The key insight is to learn a conservative Q-function that intentionally underestimates values for out-of-distribution actions so that the Q-estimate lower-bounds the true policy value, preventing spurious optimistic updates. Methodologically, Conservative Q-Learning (CQL) adds a simple Q-value regularizer to the Bellman error objective that penalizes Q-values of actions sampled from a broad set (e.g., policy and dataset actions) while preserving accuracy on dataset actions; this regularizer can be implemented on top of existing deep Q-learning or actor-critic algorithms and is shown theoretically to produce a value lower bound and empirically to yield substantially better returns across discrete and continuous benchmarks.

The paper addresses the relationship between Transformers and structured state-space models (SSMs), motivated by recent empirical results showing SSMs can rival Transformers for language modeling and the need for more efficient architectures. Its key insight is that Transformers, various attention mechanisms, and SSMs can be unified through decompositions of structured semiseparable matrices, revealing a state-space duality (SSD) that exposes equivalent computational primitives across these model families. Leveraging SSD, the authors derive generalized models and efficient algorithms that blend selective SSM behavior with attention-like operations, and they instantiate this as Mamba-2: a refinement of the Mamba selective SSM that implements the dual formulations to achieve 2–8× speedups while retaining competitive language-modeling performance.

The paper addresses the communication bottleneck in distributed stochastic optimization caused by contractive (biased) compressors like Top-K, for which the standard remedy—error feedback (EF)—has limitations in theory and practice. The key insight is that any contractive compressor can be transformed into an induced unbiased compressor, enabling the use of the richer set of algorithms and analyses available for unbiased compression rather than relying on EF. Methodologically, the authors construct a transformation that produces an unbiased compressor from a given contractive one, prove improved memory, communication-complexity, and assumption requirements (including extensions to federated learning with arbitrary partial participation), and validate these theoretical gains with experiments showing better performance than EF.

The paper studies why fast single-step adversarial training with FGSM can suddenly fail—“catastrophic overfitting”—losing robustness during training, and questions whether the commonly used random initialization fixes the issue. The key insight is that randomness only helps by shrinking effective perturbation size and that catastrophic overfitting arises from local nonlinearity (even in tiny networks or a single filter) which makes the FGSM linear approximation invalid. To address this, the authors introduce GradAlign, a regularizer that maximizes alignment of input gradients within the perturbation set so the FGSM perturbation better matches multi-step solutions, thereby preventing overfitting and enabling effective fast adversarial training for larger ℓ∞ radii. Experiments show GradAlign narrows the robustness gap to multi-step methods while keeping training efficient.

The paper addresses limitations in knowledge graph link prediction where typical embedding-based models combine entity and relation vectors with simple additive or concatenation-based interactions, which cannot express relation-specific projections of source entities. The key insight is to treat relations as context that generates the parameters of the function applied to source-entity embeddings, enabling richer, relation-conditioned transformations instead of fixed, shared matrices. Concretely, the authors use relation embeddings to parameterize (generate) parts of the scoring model applied to entity embeddings and integrate this contextual parameter generation into two existing link-prediction architectures—including the prior state-of-the-art—thereby increasing representational capacity. This approach yields significant accuracy improvements, sets a new state-of-the-art on benchmarks, and speeds convergence by up to 28×.

The paper tackles the limited data efficiency and expressivity of graph neural networks for predicting molecular and tensorial properties, which arises in part from using rotation-invariant representations that discard directional information. Its key insight is that enforcing rotational equivariance in message passing—so node features transform appropriately under rotations—retains essential geometric information and boosts learning efficiency and accuracy while allowing compact models. The authors introduce PaiNN, a polarizable atom interaction neural network that uses equivariant atom-wise features and equivariant message and update functions to predict scalar and tensorial quantities, demonstrating improved benchmark performance, smaller/faster models, and leveraging the learned representations to predict tensor properties and molecular spectra. Applied to spectrum simulation, PaiNN achieves 4–5 orders of magnitude speedup over electronic structure calculations while maintaining accuracy.

The paper investigates why recent methods for pruning neural networks at initialization (SNIP, GraSP, SynFlow) fail to match the post-training accuracy of simple magnitude-based pruning, diagnosing whether their per-weight saliency decisions truly matter. The key insight is that these initialization-time algorithms do not depend meaningfully on which specific weights they remove: randomly shuffling pruning masks within layers or reinitializing weights preserves or improves accuracy, implying only the per-layer pruning fraction matters. Methodologically, the authors empirically evaluate and compare these pruning schemes across networks and datasets, perform controlled mask-shuffling and reinitialization experiments, and show that layer-wise sparsity profiles—rather than individual weight rankings—explain most of the performance, calling into question the heuristics used to justify pruning at initialization.

The paper addresses active learning for deep neural networks in realistic streaming scenarios where data arrive sequentially and labels must be requested on the fly rather than from an offline pool. Its key insight is that effective streaming active learning can be achieved by balancing per-sample uncertainty with diversity among a small group of recently seen points, thereby matching a target query rate without hand-tuned hyperparameters. The proposed method, VeSSAL, examines incoming data in small batches, scores candidates by a combined uncertainty-diversity objective, selects a subset to query immediately to satisfy the query budget, and updates the model incrementally; this streaming sampling scheme enables practical batch active learning for DNNs on large, fragmented, or human-in-the-loop datasets.

The paper tackles the challenge of enlarging convolutional neural networks' receptive fields without blowing up parameter counts or training difficulty, noting that standard large kernels are expensive and fixed-pattern dilated convolutions (DC) underperform. The key insight is to make the sparse kernel sampling pattern itself learnable—allowing the positions (spacings) of the nonzero kernel taps to be optimized via backpropagation using an interpolation scheme—so the model can adapt where to sample information rather than being constrained to a regular grid. Methodologically, the authors introduce Dilated Convolution with Learnable Spacings (DCLS), a general n-D formulation that replaces fixed DC by parameterizing tap locations and interpolating weights at those continuous positions; they show drop-in replacement of convolutions in ResNet50 and depthwise convolutions in ConvNeXt yields improved ImageNet accuracy and downstream/robustness gains at iso-parameters (with negligible throughput cost in separable-convolution architectures), whereas classic DC performs poorly.

The paper addresses the failure of 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) to produce high-quality, real-time neural renderings in large-scale scenes because Structure-from-Motion (SfM) initializations are sparse or missing on texture-less surfaces, leading to poor optimization and rendering. The key insight is to borrow multi-view stereo (MVS) priors and progressive propagation to densify Gaussians more accurately than the naive split-and-clone heuristics, using existing reconstructed geometry and patch matching to guide placement and orientation of new primitives. The method, GaussianPro, iteratively propagates Gaussians by identifying reliable geometry, performing patch-based correspondences across views, and spawning new Gaussians with informed positions and normals, then optimizing the expanded set for rendering. Experiments on both large- and small-scale scenes, notably the Waymo dataset, demonstrate substantially improved reconstruction and a 1.15 dB PSNR gain over baseline 3DGS.

The paper addresses the challenge in offline reinforcement learning of improving a policy beyond the behavior policy without querying Q-values for out-of-distribution (OOD) actions, which induces large errors from distributional shift. The key insight is that the recently popular in-sample learning paradigm (e.g., IQL) can be understood as performing Implicit Value Regularization (IVR): by construction it regularizes value estimates implicitly so the policy improves using only actions seen in the data, avoiding OOD queries. Building on this view, the authors derive two practical in-sample algorithms—Sparse Q-learning (SQL) and Exponential Q-learning (EQL)—that implement IVR-style regularizers fully within the dataset (introducing sparsity to the value learning to improve robustness to noisy data) and empirically demonstrate their advantages over prior methods like IQL and CQL on D4RL benchmarks, especially in small or noisy data regimes.

The paper addresses why state space models (SSMs), despite favorable theoretical scaling, lag behind attention-based Transformers in language modeling both in expressivity and hardware efficiency. The key insight is that existing SSMs fail mainly at recalling distant tokens and comparing tokens across a sequence—capabilities central to language modeling—and that a specialized SSM layer plus better implementation can close both the quality and speed gaps. To that end the authors introduce H3, an SSM layer explicitly designed for recall and cross-token comparison which matches attention on synthetic tasks and nearly matches or surpasses Transformers on real language benchmarks when used in hybrid models; and they introduce FlashConv, a fused-block FFT and state-passing implementation that greatly improves runtime and long-sequence scaling, enabling faster generation and competitive or superior perplexity and few-shot performance at up to multi-billion parameter scales.

The paper tackles the problem of reducing communication in distributed stochastic gradient methods while retaining fast convergence when using general (possibly biased) gradient compressors, where naive compression creates persistent errors that slow or break convergence and it was unknown whether error compensation can be combined with Nesterov-style acceleration. The key insight is that error compensation can be incorporated into an accelerated variance-reduced framework in a way that controls the compression error and preserves accelerated linear rates under standard smoothness and strong-convexity assumptions. Concretely, the authors design an error-compensated loopless Katyusha algorithm that maintains and corrects compression residuals while applying the loopless accelerated variance-reduction updates, and they prove an accelerated linear convergence bound for any compressor satisfying a contraction property. Empirically, the method achieves the same optimization accuracy with substantially fewer communication rounds than prior error-compensated algorithms, demonstrating that acceleration and error feedback are compatible in practice.

The paper addresses the problem of Catastrophic Overfitting (CO) in single-step adversarial training—where models trained with FGSM suddenly become vulnerable to multi-step attacks—seeking a reliable and efficient remedy that scales to large perturbation radii. The key insight is that stronger random noise injected around the clean input combined with deliberately not clipping the perturbed example prior to the FGSM step prevents CO even for large epsilons, contradicting prior beliefs that mild noise or clipping were sufficient or necessary. Building on this, the authors propose Noise-FGSM (N-FGSM), which adds a carefully scaled random perturbation and then applies a single FGSM update without clipping, and they empirically show across many experiments that N-FGSM matches or outperforms the more expensive GradAlign regularizer while being about three times faster.

The paper addresses the challenge of modeling transitive relations in knowledge graph embeddings, a common relation pattern that many existing models struggle to capture alongside symmetry, asymmetry, inversion and composition. Its key insight is that transitivity can be represented using projection operations, and that combining projection with relational rotations yields a representation expressive enough to infer all the major relation patterns. The proposed Rot-Pro method implements this by projecting entity embeddings into relation-specific subspaces and applying rotations to model relational transformations, with theoretical proofs that the architecture can represent symmetry, asymmetry, inversion, composition and transitivity. Empirically, Rot-Pro better learns transitive patterns and achieves state-of-the-art link prediction performance on datasets rich in transitive relations.

result.text: The paper addresses why iterative magnitude pruning (IMP) can find sparse “winning ticket” subnetworks that match full-network accuracy and what information a final trained mask encodes for rewound networks. The key insight is that at high sparsities, successive pruned networks are matching exactly when they are connected by a linear, zero-error path, meaning the final mask selects an axial subspace that intersects a desired linearly connected mode of a matching error sublevel set, and that SGD’s robustness lets it return to that mode despite early perturbations. Methodologically, the authors analyze the geometry of the error landscape to link mask identity, linear connectivity of error minima, and landscape flatness to limits on per-iteration pruning, and they empirically and theoretically show retraining’s role is primarily to produce new small weights to prune while SGD navigates back to the same mode.

The paper addresses the lack of theory-driven methods in deep active learning by linking sample selection to models’ generalization rather than relying on ad-hoc heuristics. Its key insight is that, under an ultra-wide neural network regime, faster training convergence correlates with better generalization, so actively selecting samples that maximize training dynamics will improve final performance. The method, dynamicAL, formalizes this connection, proves the positive correlation between convergence speed and generalization, and then operationalizes sample selection by optimizing training-dynamics-based objectives with two computational relaxations that reduce subset-selection time from polynomial to constant, yielding a scalable algorithm that empirically outperforms prior baselines on large networks and datasets.

The paper studies how convolution and pooling in kernel methods affect approximation and generalization for image-like data, addressing the gap in precise understanding of their interplay in convolutional architectures. Its key insight is that for inputs uniformly on the hypercube a complete, exact characterization of the RKHS of a single-layer convolution+pooling+downsampling kernel enables closed-form asymptotic expressions for the generalization error of any target function in high dimension. Methodologically, the authors derive the RKHS by analyzing how convolution enforces locality and pooling enforces approximate translation invariance, then use this spectral characterization to compute sharp sample-complexity rates and quantify the improvement in learning efficiency due to locality and pooling versus unfettered (global) kernels. The results give a precise trade-off description between approximation power and generalization gains induced by one-layer convolutional kernels.

result.text: The paper addresses offline reinforcement learning, where learning from a fixed dataset risks overestimating out-of-distribution (OOD) actions and thus requires conservative value estimates, but excessive pessimism hurts generalization and performance. The key insight is that conservatism should be “mild”: rather than harshly penalizing or strictly regularizing away OOD actions, the algorithm should actively train OOD actions with appropriately assigned pseudo-Q values to prevent erroneous overestimation while preserving generalization. The authors propose Mildly Conservative Q-learning (MCQ), which assigns and trains on pseudo Q-values for OOD actions, provides theoretical guarantees that the induced policy is no worse than the behavior policy and avoids OOD overestimation, and empirically outperforms prior methods on D4RL benchmarks while transferring more effectively to online fine-tuning.

The paper investigates the theoretical expressive capacity of linear state space models (SSMs) for language modeling, comparing their formal-language abilities to transformers and traditional RNNs to clarify what tasks they can or cannot represent. The key insight is that SSMs and transformers have overlapping but distinct strengths: SSMs can implement exact, simple solutions for "star-free" state-tracking problems and can represent bounded hierarchical structures with optimal memory usage without needing an explicit stack, yet a common design choice in current SSMs restricts their full expressive power. Methodologically, the authors analyze formal language classes and state-tracking tasks to derive provable capabilities and limitations of SSMs, discuss architectural implications, and validate their theoretical findings empirically on a recent SSM model (Mamba).

The paper addresses the problem of stabilizing and accelerating distributed training under contractive communication compression (e.g., Top-k) where the popular error feedback (EF) heuristic lacks satisfactory theory or practical performance without strong or impractical assumptions. Its key insight is a redesigned error-feedback mechanism (EF21) that corrects the deficiencies of prior analyses by using a different compressor-correction scheme that can be analyzed under standard assumptions in the heterogeneous-data distributed setting, yielding provably faster rates without resorting to unbiased compressors or bounded-gradient hypotheses. Methodologically, the authors propose the EF21 algorithm which modifies how compression errors are accumulated and compensated across workers, prove an O(1/T) convergence rate for smooth nonconvex objectives (improving over the previous O(1/T^{2/3}) guarantee) and show linear convergence under the PL condition, and validate that EF21 consistently outperforms classical EF in experiments.

The paper addresses robust overfitting in adversarial training, where networks fit adversarial examples on the training set but generalize poorly to test data, and seeks theoretical generalization guarantees despite the nonsmooth outer maximization defining adversarial loss. The key insight is that although the adversarial (outer) loss is nonsmooth, it satisfies an η-approximate smoothness property with η depending on the perturbation magnitude ε, which lets one extend uniform stability analyses to this setting. Methodologically, the authors prove stability-based generalization bounds for SGD on the class of η-approximate smooth functions (thereby covering adversarial loss), showing that robust test error degrades with ε as training time T grows—between Ω(ε√T) and O(εT)—and they theoretically characterize how practices like early stopping, cyclic learning rates, and stochastic weight averaging improve stability and thus mitigate robust overfitting.

Its key insight is that compositions of Householder transformations—specifically parameterizing relations with sequences of Householder rotations and projections—provide a more expressive, theoretically grounded family of linear transformations that can model those patterns and mapping behaviors in high-dimensional spaces. The proposed HousE framework represents relations as learnable products of Householder rotation matrices to flexibly encode pattern structure and Householder-based projection operators to handle mapping multiplicity, generalizing rotation-based models by extending rotations beyond low-dimensional complex planes; experiments show HousE attains state-of-the-art results across five standard benchmarks.

Methodologically, the authors develop general SE(3)-equivariant operations and building blocks for deep networks on geometric point clouds, train these models to reconstruct molecular wavefunctions and densities, and demonstrate orders-of-magnitude speedups and large error reductions versus prior work, enabling end-to-end property derivation, transfer learning to correct lower-level references, and use of predicted wavefunctions as high-quality initial guesses for conventional quantum chemistry solvers.

result.text: The paper tackles offline reinforcement learning, where the challenge is to learn reliable policies from fixed logged data without environment interaction, focusing on avoiding overoptimistic behavior in regions poorly covered by the dataset. Its key insight is to cast model-based offline RL as a two-player zero-sum game in which an adversarial dynamics model is trained to both fit the dataset and minimize the policy’s estimated value, thereby inducing pessimism where the data is scarce. The method, RAMBO, alternates between policy optimization inside the learned model and adversarial model updates that trade off data likelihood with value minimization, yielding a conservative value estimate that provably lower-bounds true performance under PAC-style guarantees. Empirically, RAMBO achieves stronger and more robust performance than prior state-of-the-art offline RL baselines on standard benchmarks.

The paper addresses the challenge of making Transformer models both high-quality and efficient on long sequences by revisiting architectural choices that limit performance and speed. The proposed method, FLASH, replaces standard multi-head attention with gated attention units and a tailored linear approximation that preserves essential attention behavior while enabling linear-time computation; this design matches improved Transformer perplexities at 512 and 8K contexts while delivering substantial training speedups (up to ~12×) on large language modeling benchmarks.

args.text: We propose a temporal rule-conditioned Householder hyper-rotation model for temporal KG forecasting that unifies time-conditioned rotations with interpretable symbolic priors. A hypernetwork conditioned on (relation, timestamp) and embeddings of top supporting temporal rules generates a product of Householder reflections and projection operators that act on head-entity embeddings; the reflections capture relation–time dynamics while the projections encode transitive/compositional subspaces. Training jointly optimizes link prediction with a differentiable rule-satisfaction loss and a temporal-consistency regularizer, enabling both stronger generalization to future times and human-readable attributions from reflections to activated rules. result.text: The paper addresses the limitation of common spatial up-sampling operators (interpolation, transposed conv, un-pooling) which rely on local pixel relationships and thus struggle to capture global dependencies for multi-scale modeling. The key insight is that up-sampling can be more globally and theoretically grounded in the Fourier domain via spectral convolution principles, but requires explicit transform rules because Fourier-domain features do not obey local-similarity properties of spatial features. The proposed Deep Fourier Up-Sampling (FourierUp) operator implements this by transforming low-resolution feature maps with a 2D discrete Fourier transform, applying novel Fourier-domain dimension-increase rules to expand spectral representations consistently across resolutions, and mapping back with an inverse 2D Fourier transform; FourierUp is plug-and-play and improves performance across tasks like detection, segmentation, de-raining, dehazing, and guided super-resolution.

args.text: Posterior-Consensus 3DGS (PC-3GS) is a distributed training scheme that treats each Gaussian’s parameters as a probabilistic posterior and fuses workers via uncertainty-weighted consensus rather than raw parameter averaging. Each shard runs SGLD-based updates to maintain per-parameter means/variances and communicates only low-rank sufficient statistics for Gaussians whose projected pixels cross shard boundaries; a master (or peer-to-peer ADMM) penalizes KL divergence between local and global marginals, weighting constraints by inverse variance to naturally prioritize confident updates. Partitioning and sparse all-to-all follow Grendel, while spatial blocking and ADMM-style consensus follow DOGS; MVS-guided priors initialize means/variances in texture-poor regions to stabilize early training. This yields lower bandwidth, better robustness to poor initialization, and improved quality on large scenes by aligning a product-of-experts posterior across shards.

result.text: The paper tackles the problem of pruning neural networks more effectively by accounting for the joint impact of removing multiple weights rather than treating each weight independently or relying on simple magnitude heuristics. Its key insight is that pruning decisions should consider how weights cancel or interact with one another, extending the Optimal Brain Surgeon (OBS) idea to a combinatorial setting where groups of weights are selected for simultaneous removal and the remaining weights are adjusted accordingly. Methodologically, the authors propose a tractable heuristic to approximate this combinatorial OBS selection and a systematic weight-update rule for compensating the removal, demonstrating that their joint-selection approach yields better performance at high sparsity and that the post-pruning update improves results even when paired with other pruning strategies.

The paper tackles the problem of reducing computation, storage, and communication during gradient-based training by updating only a sparse subset of a neural network’s parameters across iterations. The key insight is that a fixed mask selecting the parameters with the largest Fisher information provides a simple, effective proxy for which weights matter most for the task, so those parameters can be the only ones updated repeatedly. The method builds a sparse mask by computing Fisher scores for parameters, selecting the top-k, and then training while keeping all other weights frozen; experiments on transfer learning and distributed training show this fixed-Fisher-mask approach matches or outperforms existing sparse-update methods while lowering memory and communication overhead.

The paper addresses the challenge of efficiently estimating and enforcing Lipschitz constants for convolutional neural networks—a problem important for training stability, generalization, and adversarial robustness but whose exact computation is NP-hard. The key insight is that convolutional layers can be analyzed via the theory of Toeplitz matrices, which lets one derive a new spectral-norm upper bound for convolution operators that is simultaneously tighter than commonly used easy bounds and much cheaper to compute than exact or costly approximations. Methodologically, the authors translate convolutional kernels into structured Toeplitz (or block-Toeplitz) matrices, derive computable spectral bounds from their properties, and incorporate this bound into a practical training algorithm that constrains or regularizes layers to satisfy Lipschitz constraints.

The paper addresses the challenge of generative modeling for discrete biological sequences, where standard continuous diffusion/SDE-based score models are not naturally suited to discrete data or hard constraints. The key insight is to define a continuous-time diffusion process on the probability simplex whose stationary distribution is a Dirichlet—so samples remain simplex-valued and naturally represent categorical distributions over tokens—yielding a principled bridge between continuous score-based SDEs and discrete sequence generation. The method, called the Dirichlet Diffusion Score Model, trains a score-based network to denoise simplex-valued trajectories under this Dirichlet SDE, enabling conditional sampling that enforces hard constraints (demonstrated on Sudoku generation and solving) and application to biology, where it produces human promoter DNA sequences with properties similar to natural promoters.

The paper tackles the bottleneck of quadratic-cost attention in Transformers that limits context length and scaling, aiming to build a dense-attention-free operator that matches Transformer performance at long sequences. The key insight is that long-range sequence modeling can be achieved by interleaving implicitly parameterized long convolutions with data-controlled gating—providing expressive, efficiently computable global receptive fields without relying on attention or expensive state-space machinery. The method, called Hyena, implements subquadratic long convolutions via implicit parameterization and fast convolution algorithms combined with gating, and it is evaluated on recall, reasoning, and language modeling tasks where it outperforms prior implicit/explicit alternatives, matches dense-attention models while reducing compute (≈20% at 2K) and dramatically improving speed at very long sequence lengths.

result.text: The paper addresses why adversarial training suffers from robust overfitting and its puzzling dependence on perturbation radius and data quality by identifying a previously overlooked source of error: label noise. The key insight is that adversarial perturbations distort the true label distribution of examples, so inheriting the original clean labels for adversarial counterparts introduces label noise that fuels overfitting and explains epoch-wise double descent. Methodologically, the authors analyze this label-mismatch theoretically and empirically and propose an automatic label-calibration scheme that adjusts labels for adversarial examples to counteract the noise, yielding consistent robustness improvements across models and datasets without extra hyperparameters or tuning.

The paper addresses reducing uplink communication in federated learning under realistic challenges—partial client participation and heterogeneous data—while handling the distortion introduced by communication compression. Its key insight is that the classical stochastic controlled averaging (SCA) can be reformulated into an equivalent but simpler and more communication-efficient implementation that halves uplink cost and serves as a foundation for compression-aware algorithms. Building on that reformulation, the authors develop two algorithms—SCALLION for unbiased compressors and SCAFCOM for biased compressors—that integrate compressed updates without extra assumptions on compression error or limits on heterogeneity, and they prove improved communication and computation complexity relative to prior work. Empirically, both methods match full-precision FL performance with much less uplink transmission and beat recent compressed-FL baselines under the same communication budget.

The paper tackles temporal knowledge graph completion (TKGC), the problem of predicting missing time-stamped facts in a knowledge graph by leveraging learned latent representations of entities, relations, and times. The proposed model, BoxTE, adapts the static BoxE architecture by incorporating timestamp-specific transformations and boxes that represent when facts hold, training these embeddings to score triples with timestamps so that correct temporal facts lie in appropriate boxes; theoretical analysis proves expressiveness and empirical evaluation across benchmarks shows state-of-the-art performance.

args.text: We propose Streaming-BAIT, an on-the-fly active learner that brings BAIT’s Fisher-information MLE-error objective to the streaming regime by maintaining a low-rank sketch of the empirical Fisher over a moving window and selecting queries that maximize incremental Fisher gain under a rolling budget. To keep selection and training cheap, we restrict both sketching and gradient updates to a fixed Fisher mask of top-importance parameters and inject diversity by greedy selection in the sketch’s basis, mirroring scalable large-batch diversification. A lightweight controller balances per-sample uncertainty with marginal Fisher gain to meet a target query rate, and uses a training-dynamics signal to reweight the sketch so directions associated with faster convergence receive higher priority. This yields a compute-efficient streaming active learning algorithm with principled Fisher objectives, scalable selection, and improved label efficiency.

result.text: The paper tackles the problem of making neural architecture search (NAS) fast and broadly applicable to diverse, under-explored domains beyond computer vision, where AutoML could have the most impact. The key insight is that fixing a standard CNN topology but searching only over operation choices—specifically kernel sizes and dilations—gives rich multi-resolution feature extraction while dramatically reducing the search space, and that leveraging the Fourier diagonalization of convolution lets one efficiently compute mixtures of these operations. Building on this, the authors propose DASH, a differentiable NAS algorithm that uses Fourier-based diagonalization to perform weight-sharing over operation mixtures with improved asymptotic complexity, yielding up to 10× faster search in practice; they evaluate DASH on ten varied tasks (e.g., PDE solving, protein folding, heart disease detection) and show it outperforms state-of-the-art AutoML on most tasks while keeping search-plus-retraining overhead low (often under 2× the training time of a baseline CNN).

result.text: The paper addresses the vulnerability of deep reinforcement learning (RL) policies to small, worst-case perturbations in high-dimensional observation spaces and questions whether current notions and defenses for adversarial robustness are appropriate for RL. The key insight is that high-sensitivity directions in the policy landscape are abundant and can be discovered by more natural, black-box methods rather than only by targeted worst-case searches, and surprisingly, standard (vanilla) training can yield policies that are more robust than those produced by state-of-the-art adversarial training. The authors analyze the policy manifold to characterize these pervasive sensitivity directions, compare black-box and white-box perturbation methods, and empirically evaluate robustness of policies trained with and without adversarial techniques, arguing that robustness definitions and defense methods for deep RL must be rethought to account for these findings.

result.text: The paper addresses limitations of Transformer attention—its weak inductive bias for position-aware local structure and quadratic cost—that hinder long-sequence modeling. The key insight is that adding a single-head gated attention augmented with an exponential moving average injects position-aware local dependency bias into otherwise position-agnostic attention, improving inductive bias while retaining attention’s modeling power. The method, called Mega, implements gated attention equipped with moving-average state updates and offers a chunked variant that splits sequences into fixed-length segments to reduce time and space complexity to linear with minimal quality loss; extensive experiments across long-range benchmarks, translation, language modeling, and vision/speech tasks show consistent gains over Transformer variants and state-space models.

The paper addresses the high communication cost of federated/local SGD, where occasional model averaging still requires large payloads per round for modern models. Its key insight is that combining local updates with an error-compensated double-compression scheme (and an analogous momentum variant) preserves convergence properties while dramatically reducing per-round communication. Methodologically, the authors design and analyze compressed local SGD algorithms that apply two-stage compression with error feedback to worker-to-server and server-to-worker communications, prove nonconvex convergence rates that match full-precision local SGD’s linear speedup in the number of workers while improving communication complexity, and corroborate these gains empirically.

The paper addresses why adversarial training suffers from robust overfitting and its puzzling dependence on perturbation radius and data quality by identifying a previously overlooked source of error: label noise. The key insight is that adversarial perturbations distort the true label distribution of examples, so inheriting the original clean labels for adversarial counterparts introduces label noise that fuels overfitting and explains epoch-wise double descent. Methodologically, the authors analyze this label-mismatch theoretically and empirically and propose an automatic label-calibration scheme that adjusts labels for adversarial examples to counteract the noise, yielding consistent robustness improvements across models and datasets without extra hyperparameters or tuning.

The paper addresses temporal knowledge graph completion, focusing on the challenge of predicting time-sensitive events while capturing both timeliness and causality—properties that prior methods struggle to represent simultaneously. The key insight is to combine temporal logic-derived causal rules with time-independent commonsense knowledge so that embeddings encode event causality and general plausibility separately but jointly inform predictions. Methodologically, LCGE learns time-sensitive embeddings regularized by a temporal rule-learning algorithm that extracts and enforces causal predicate relationships, and integrates auxiliary commonsense embeddings to evaluate event plausibility, yielding improved prediction accuracy and causal explainability on TKGC benchmarks.

result.text: This paper tackles the problem of efficient filter pruning for compressing convolutional neural networks without the cumbersome multi-stage training and many hyperparameters typical of prior work, and it also addresses uneven pruning needs across layers. The key insight is to learn structured sparsity directly from scratch by dynamically allocating layer-wise pruning ratios and progressively increasing a sparsity-inducing penalty so the network becomes sparse gradually rather than being forced abruptly. Methodologically, DPFPS imposes a novel structured sparsity regularizer on expected pruning parameters, uses a Taylor-series-based channel sensitivity criterion to identify pruneable channels, and solves the resulting pruning-ratio optimization with an iterative soft-thresholding (ISTA) procedure under dynamic sparsity, producing a final pruned model that requires no fine-tuning. Experiments on CIFAR and ImageNet demonstrate competitive performance with state-of-the-art methods, e.g., compressing ResNet-101 to cut 44.97% of FLOPs while slightly improving Top-5 accuracy.

args.text: Mask-Aware Active Learning aligns sample selection with constrained training by optimizing a Fisher-information bound computed on a sparse, fixed update mask. We alternate between (infrequent) mask updates that select top-k parameters by Fisher score and (frequent) batch selection that scores candidates by their incremental reduction of the masked Fisher-based MLE error bound, while adding a lightweight diversification step to avoid redundancy. This prioritizes examples whose gradients concentrate on the updatable parameters, yielding strong label efficiency under tight compute/communication budgets (e.g., federated or on-device training). The approach preserves BAIT’s theory-driven selection while integrating fixed-Fisher-mask training and scalable diversification to remain practical at large scale.

We propose SpecPos-Conv, a convolutional primitive that jointly learns a continuous, frequency-controllable kernel envelope and a compact set of continuous tap locations, executed via Fourier diagonalization to enable fast, differentiable mixtures during NAS. Concretely, we parameterize the kernel in a FlexConv-style spectral form while optimizing DCLS-like tap positions with interpolation, and embed this operator in a DASH-style supernet that searches over mixtures of spectral envelopes and tap patterns with weight sharing. To stabilize training and improve out-of-distribution generalization, we impose layerwise Lipschitz constraints using efficient Toeplitz spectral-norm bounds. For multi-scale architectures, pairing SpecPos-Conv with Fourier-domain up-sampling ensures consistent spectral scaling and alias-free transfer to higher resolutions, yielding compact models that capture long-range dependencies across non-vision domains.

result.text: The paper tackles reconstructing and real-time rendering of complex dynamic 3D scenes from 2D images by addressing limitations of neural implicit methods that struggle to capture spatio-temporal structure and to scale deformation modeling. The key insight is to treat spacetime as a single 4D volume and approximate it with explicit, learnable 4D primitives—anisotropic, rotatable 4D Gaussians that carry geometry and view-/time-varying appearance via 4D spheroidal harmonic coefficients—thereby avoiding complex deformation fields and directly encoding spatio-temporal structure. The method optimizes a collection of these 4D Gaussians end-to-end to fit input video frames, and uses a tailored splatting-style renderer to synthesize novel views at any time in real time; experiments show improved visual quality and efficiency across monocular and multi-view dynamic benchmarks.

result.text: The paper addresses the limitation of current scene text recognition (STR) systems that rely on 1D language models and thus ignore 2D spatial visual semantics within and between character instances, which hurts generalization to arbitrarily shaped text. The key insight is that modeling pixel-level spatial relations inside each character instance and across instances yields richer visual semantics that enable better textual reasoning complementary to language priors. The method builds per-character subgraphs from segmentation maps (nodes = pixels, edges = spatial similarity), links subgraph roots into a complete graph, and applies a graph convolutional network for textual reasoning (GTR) supervised with cross-entropy; GTR is plugged in parallel with a language model in a segmentation-based STR baseline (S-GTR) and trained with mutual learning. S-GTR achieves state-of-the-art results on six challenging STR benchmarks and generalizes to multi-lingual datasets.

result.text: The paper addresses how to theoretically ground and improve soft threshold pruning, a top-performing neural network pruning approach whose prior threshold-tuning strategies lacked unified explanation. The key insight is that soft threshold pruning can be reformulated as solving an implicit L1-regularized optimization problem via the Iterative Shrinkage-Thresholding Algorithm (ISTA), which reveals that different empirical threshold schedulers correspond to different ways of tuning the L1 penalty and that maintaining a stable L1 coefficient yields a time-invariant objective. Building on this view, the authors derive an optimal threshold scheduler and a family of pruning methods—including sparsify-during-training, early pruning, and pruning-at-initialization—that keep the regularization coefficient stable, and they validate the approach with state-of-the-art results on ResNet-50, MobileNet-V1 and SEW ResNet-18 on ImageNet.

args.text: We propose a compute-aware co-active learning framework that jointly selects labeled batches and a sparse parameter-update mask to maximize expected generalization gain per unit wall-clock and communication budget. Concretely, we optimize a Fisher-information–based MLE error-reduction bound restricted to a k-parameter mask (linearized/NTK regime), operationalized by alternating steps: (i) pick a fixed mask via top-k Fisher/gradient scores; (ii) choose a large, diversity-regularized batch that maximizes the restricted Fisher gain using scalable matrix sketches. This unifies Fisher-guided selection with massive-batch diversification and fixed-Fisher sparse updating, and extends naturally to streaming by maintaining a sliding-window mask and querying points whose restricted Fisher contributions cross an adaptive threshold. We hypothesize superior label efficiency under tight compute/communication budgets and propose submodular surrogates for the restricted Fisher gain to enable greedy selection with approximation guarantees.

result.text: The paper addresses the problem of providing formal robustness guarantees for reinforcement learning policies against adversarial perturbations, both in terms of per-state action stability and worst-case cumulative reward. The key insight is that smoothing techniques applied to value-based policies can certify action invariance and lower bounds on finite-horizon returns: local smoothing around states yields protections for individual actions along a trajectory, while global smoothing (and an adaptive local search variant) can produce tight certified lower bounds on cumulative rewards. The method, called CROP, instantiates these ideas for policies derived from Q-functions by developing a local smoothing algorithm to guarantee action robustness, a global smoothing algorithm to certify finite-horizon reward bounds, and an adaptive local smoothing search to tighten reward certificates, and it empirically evaluates these certificates (and their tightness) across several robust RL training methods and four environments.

result.text: The paper tackles the problem of distributed mean estimation (DME) in federated learning under heterogeneous client communication budgets and packet losses, which cause increased estimation error when gradients are lossy-compressed. The key insight is to design a compression-and-aggregation scheme that is inherently robust to differing per-client budgets and unreliable delivery, so that the server can recover an accurate global mean despite missing or differently-compressed contributions. The proposed method, EDEN, combines tailored stochastic compression operators with an encoding/decoding protocol and theoretical bias/variance analysis that account for budget heterogeneity and packet drop probabilities, yielding provable error bounds; empirical evaluations show EDEN consistently outperforms prior DME techniques in both accuracy and communication efficiency.

This paper addresses how to produce condensed (distilled) datasets that not only preserve classification accuracy but also confer adversarial robustness to models trained on them, avoiding the high cost of standard adversarial training. The key insight is that controlling the curvature of the model’s loss landscape during distillation can embed robustness into the synthetic data: lower curvature around data points makes models less sensitive to adversarial perturbations. The authors implement this by adding a curvature regularization term to the dataset distillation objective—penalizing large Hessian norms or approximations thereof—so distilled samples encourage flat, robust local minima, and show empirically that this yields models with better accuracy and robustness than models trained with conventional adversarial training while incurring much lower computational overhead.

args.text: We propose a streaming deep active learning algorithm that optimizes a Fisher-information–based MLE error bound online by maintaining a low-rank NTK-based sketch of the empirical Fisher and selecting incoming points that maximally reduce the bound subject to a small-window diversity constraint. Concretely, we amortize BAIT-style marginal-gain computations via incremental Jacobian features and rank-r Cholesky updates, and combine them with VeSSAL’s windowed diversity to avoid redundancy at target query rates. Using the NTK embedding to analyze the linearized regime, we adapt the query threshold via regret-balancing, yielding joint guarantees on regret and label requests that recover minimax rates in the linear case. This Fisher-Stream design promises stronger label efficiency than uncertainty-only streaming while remaining scalable with O(r^2) per-candidate updates and stable online operation.

result.text: The paper addresses the limitation of Fourier-based neural operators, whose computational speedups rely on FFTs and thus require equispaced rectangular grids, preventing efficient application to problems defined on arbitrary, non-equispaced point distributions. The key insight is that neural operators only need a limited set of spectral modes for sufficient expressivity, so one can avoid FFTs by directly and efficiently evaluating the underlying spectral transform on arbitrary points. The authors propose coupling an efficient implementation of direct spectral evaluations with existing neural operator architectures, enabling spectral computations on non-equispaced domains; this approach yields significant training-speed gains over baselines while matching or improving the accuracy of Fourier neural operators in extensive empirical tests.

args.text: OT-Consensus 3DGS aligns and fuses overlapping local Gaussian sets to a global model via visibility-aware optimal transport (OT), avoiding brittle parameter-wise equality assumptions that break under cloning/splitting and heterogeneous partitions. We define a transport cost that combines 3D center/covariance distances, SH-appearance distance, and view-weighted opacity overlap; matched pairs are merged by uncertainty-weighted barycenters while unmatched mass spawns/prunes components, yielding identity-agnostic consensus. Implemented atop Grendel’s sparse all-to-all and DOGS’s spatial blocking, we solve entropic OT only for Gaussians whose projected pixels co-occur and warm-start with k-NN, keeping overhead low and reducing duplication/oscillations. Compared to ADMM or posterior-averaging consensus, OT-Consensus produces a more compact, well-aligned global mixture and improves large-scene PSNR/LPIPS at similar bandwidth.

result.text: This paper addresses the problem of certifying robustness of offline reinforcement learning against training-time poisoning attacks, where an adversary can arbitrarily manipulate a subset of training trajectories. The key insight is that by defining tractable certification criteria tailored to RL—per-state action stability and cumulative reward bounds—and by using aggregation and partitioning protocols over trajectories, one can provably bound how many poisoned trajectories a learned policy can tolerate. The authors introduce COPA, a certification framework that computes these bounds, proposes temporal and other aggregation schemes to improve robustness, and analyzes the computational limits (showing some certification variants are tight while others are NP-complete). Empirical results across algorithms and environments show the proposed aggregation methods substantially boost certified robustness and that certification tightness and tolerable poisoning vary by algorithm and environment.

The paper tackles the quadratic time and memory bottleneck of self-attention in Transformers for long-context language modeling by replacing softmax attention with a scalable alternative. The key insight is that high-degree polynomial attention can match softmax’s modeling power while admitting efficient linear-time computation via randomized polynomial sketching from numerical linear algebra, avoiding attention sparsification and providing provable approximation guarantees. Methodologically, the authors develop sketching techniques to compress polynomial feature maps, a block-based algorithm to enforce causal masking, and integrate these into PolySketchFormer—a practical Transformer that implements linear-time polynomial attention with theoretical bounds—and validate it on synthetic and real datasets (PG19, Wikipedia, C4), demonstrating 2.5–4× training speedups at 32k context lengths versus FlashAttention without quality loss.

args.text: We propose Loss- and Participation-Aware Bias–Variance Compression (LP-BVC) for federated/distributed SGD with partial client participation and unreliable links. Using the EF-BV framework, each client adaptively selects a compressor along the bias–variance frontier (e.g., switching between EF21-style error-feedback and induced-unbiased transforms) to minimize a per-round surrogate of convergence error that accounts for its local gradient variance, participation probability, and drop rate. The server aggregates via an EDEN-like decoding that is robust to heterogeneous budgets and packet loss, and maintains control-variate statistics to stabilize the adaptively changing compressors across rounds. We hypothesize linear convergence under PL and improved communication/sample complexity versus fixed-compressor baselines in lossy, sparse-participation regimes, and provide a practical policy (a one-step lookahead minimizing predicted MSE of the global update) for compressor selection.

result.text: The paper studies whether Sharpness-Aware Minimization (SAM), which perturbs model weights to seek flat minima and improve generalization, can also confer adversarial robustness typically achieved by Adversarial Training (AT) that perturbs inputs. The key insight is a duality between SAM and AT: by smoothing the loss landscape SAM implicitly encourages features and solutions that are less sensitive to input perturbations, so it can learn more robust representations even though it does not perturb inputs. Methodologically, the authors analyze this connection both theoretically and empirically, showing that SAM alone improves adversarial robustness across experiments without degrading clean accuracy, and they compare SAM and AT variants to characterize when SAM can substitute for AT.

The key insight is to learn transferable local electronic representations via graph-based message passing that connect molecular orbitals to covalent bonds, enabling embeddings that capture local electronic structure common to multiple molecules. The paper tackles hardware-aware structural pruning: how to remove filters from neural networks to maximize accuracy while meeting a device-specific latency budget. The key insight is to combine a fast-to-evaluate global saliency score (estimating accuracy loss) with a latency lookup table (estimating per-filter latency reduction) and cast pruning as a reward-maximization resource allocation problem. Methodologically, they reformulate global structural pruning as a constrained knapsack-like optimization and solve it with an augmented knapsack solver that selects filters to drop based on joint latency and saliency rewards, yielding efficient pruning that outperforms prior methods across classification and detection benchmarks and multiple target platforms.

We propose a compute-aware co-active learning framework that jointly selects labeled batches and a sparse parameter-update mask to maximize expected generalization gain per unit wall-clock and communication budget. Concretely, we optimize a Fisher-information–based MLE error-reduction bound restricted to a k-parameter mask (linearized/NTK regime), operationalized by alternating steps: (i) pick a fixed mask via top-k Fisher/gradient scores; (ii) choose a large, diversity-regularized batch that maximizes the restricted Fisher gain using scalable matrix sketches. Each round, a small anchor set sends near-uncompressed or induced-unbiased references that define a variance-reduced control variate at the server, while miners transmit highly compressed contractive updates with error-feedback; by transforming miners’ compressors into induced-unbiased ones and analyzing them within the EF-BV framework, the server attains low-bias aggregation and linear convergence under heterogeneity. result.text: We propose Loss- and Participation-Aware Bias–Variance Compression (LP-BVC) for federated/distributed SGD with partial client participation and unreliable links. Using the EF-BV framework, each client adaptively selects a compressor along the bias–variance frontier (e.g., switching between EF21-style error-feedback and induced-unbiased transforms) to minimize a per-round surrogate of convergence error that accounts for its local gradient variance, participation probability, and drop rate. The server aggregates via an EDEN-like decoding that is robust to heterogeneous budgets and packet loss, and maintains control-variate statistics to stabilize the adaptively changing compressors across rounds. We hypothesize linear convergence under PL and improved communication/sample complexity versus fixed-compressor baselines in lossy, sparse-participation regimes, and provide a practical policy (a one-step lookahead minimizing predicted MSE of the global update) for compressor selection.

result.text: The paper studies whether Sharpness-Aware Minimization (SAM), which perturbs model weights to seek flat minima and improve generalization, can also confer adversarial robustness typically achieved by Adversarial Training (AT) that perturbs inputs. The key insight is a duality between SAM and AT: by smoothing the loss landscape SAM implicitly encourages features and solutions that are less sensitive to input perturbations, so it can learn more robust representations even though it does not perturb inputs. Methodologically, the authors analyze this connection both theoretically and empirically, showing that SAM alone improves adversarial robustness across experiments without degrading clean accuracy, and they compare SAM and AT variants to characterize when SAM can substitute for AT.

ChronoR addresses temporal link prediction on temporal knowledge graphs, a challenging problem due to non-stationary, heterogeneous data and complex temporal dependencies. Its key insight is to model relation- and time-conditioned interactions as k-dimensional rotations so that applying a learned rotation to a head-entity embedding moves it close to the corresponding tail embedding, thereby naturally encoding temporal and multi-relational dynamics. The method jointly learns dense embeddings for entities, relations, and time and parameterizes a rotation operator in high-dimensional space for each (relation, time) pair; training minimizes distance between rotated heads and tails so the model captures rich temporal–relational interactions and outperforms prior state-of-the-art methods on benchmark temporal KG link prediction tasks.

result.text: We propose a gauge- and space-group–equivariant graph neural operator that predicts k-dependent Bloch Hamiltonians H(k) for crystalline materials directly from atomic structures. To remain efficient, we use Cartesian tensor embeddings with irrep-wise processing and hard-impose Hermiticity, time-reversal, and lattice periodicity; training uses k-point sampling with band-structure and density-of-states losses. This yields symmetry-consistent surrogates for tight-binding and ab initio band structures that generalize across materials and unit-cell choices.

result.text: The paper tackles the problem of choosing layerwise sparsity for magnitude-based neural network pruning, where prior work relies on heuristics or costly hyperparameter searches and performance depends critically on per-layer sparsity allocation. Their key insight is that pruning decisions should account for each layer’s contribution to the model-level ℓ2 distortion, so weight magnitudes can be rescaled into an importance score that reflects the global impact of removing parameters. They propose LAMP (layer-adaptive magnitude-based pruning), a simple, hyperparameter-free scoring scheme that rescales magnitudes by layer-level statistics to produce layerwise sparsities for global pruning, and show empirically on image classification tasks (including weight-rewinding setups) that LAMP consistently outperforms popular baselines. The method is lightweight to compute and requires no expensive tuning while yielding better sparsity–performance tradeoffs than existing layerwise allocation strategies.

The paper tackles the question of which unlabeled examples to query in active learning by directly linking selection to downstream test performance: it proves that choosing unlabeled samples with larger gradient norms yields a tighter upper bound on test loss and thus better generalization. The key insight is that gradient norm of an example—reflecting how much it would change model parameters if labeled—predicts its value for reducing test error, but since true gradients require labels, the authors approximate them using two schemes. They propose expected-gradnorm, which estimates gradient norm via an expected empirical loss over label distributions, and entropy-gradnorm, which uses an unsupervised entropy-based surrogate, and combine both into a unified active learning framework that outperforms prior methods on image classification, semantic segmentation, and noisy cellular imaging tasks.

args.text: I propose Learnable Nonuniform Spectral Grids (LNSG) for neural operator layers on irregular domains. Instead of fixing Fourier modes or relying on equispaced FFTs, we parameterize a compact set of complex frequency locations and windowed basis functions that are optimized end-to-end, evaluating them directly at arbitrary points via differentiable nonuniform spectral transforms; a DCLS-style continuous parameterization and interpolation over frequency positions enables stable spacing learning, while FlexConv-inspired spectral regularization controls bandwidth and aliasing. Combined with a transform-once pipeline operating entirely in the learned spectral domain and hybrid local operator augmentations, LNSG captures both long-range couplings and sharp local features with fewer modes and without grid constraints. We hypothesize improved accuracy–efficiency tradeoffs on PDE benchmarks with complex geometries and variable sampling (e.g., turbulent Navier–Stokes on irregular meshes and coastal shallow-water equations).

result.text: Motion-Consistent OT Consensus scales 4D Gaussian Splatting by distributing training across overlapping spatio-temporal blocks and periodically fusing them via a visibility- and motion-aware optimal transport in 4D. The transport cost couples 4D center/covariance distances with short-horizon motion consistency (from optical flow or learned scene flow) and time-varying appearance similarity, merging matched Gaussians by uncertainty-weighted barycenters while spawning/pruning unmatched mass to avoid identity conflicts at block/time boundaries. Built atop Grendel-style sparse all-to-all and DOGS-style blocking, this identity-agnostic fusion reduces duplication and temporal flicker near motion discontinuities and improves coherence without relying on deformation fields. An asynchronous variant fuses whenever shards report, maintaining bandwidth comparable to parameter-wise consensus while remaining robust to heterogeneous devices.
