args.text: Offline RL must be conservative to avoid OOD overestimation, yet we increasingly need certified robustness to observation perturbations; we propose Certificate-Calibrated Conservative Offline RL (C3-ORL), which couples in-sample/value-conservative learning with randomized-smoothing-based certificates. C3-ORL learns a smoothed Q and policy by injecting noise around dataset states, computes per-state certified action/return lower bounds via policy/value smoothing, and then adaptively scales a CQL-style conservatism penalty and restricts policy improvement to in-dataset actions proportional to the local certified radius/density. This makes each update monotone in a certified return lower bound, yielding guarantees against L2-bounded observation attacks while avoiding excessive pessimism where robustness is high. Empirically, C3-ORL aims to improve robust returns and transfer in adversarially perturbed D4RL settings over RORL, CQL, and IVR.

result.text: Samba tackles the challenge of building language models that can handle effectively unlimited context without quadratic cost or poor length extrapolation by combining state-space compression with local attention. The key insight is to layer-wise hybridize a selective State Space Model (Mamba) that compresses and carries long-range recurrent hidden states with a Sliding Window Attention (SWA) that precisely recalls recent context, yielding both efficient long-term memory and exact short-term retrieval. Methodologically, Samba stacks Mamba and SWA in each layer so sequences are selectively summarized into recurrent states while recent tokens remain accessible via attention, and the resulting architecture is scaled to 3.8B parameters trained on 3.2T tokens; it achieves strong zero-shot and finetuned extrapolation (up to 1M and 256K contexts), superior retrieval performance on tasks like Passkey and Phonebook, and substantial throughput and generation speedups versus full-attention Transformers.

The paper addresses communication bottlenecks in distributed/federated optimization by unifying two previously separate approaches for gradient compression—variance-reduced unbiased compressors (DIANA) and error-feedback for biased contractive compressors (EF21)—into a single framework that can handle both. The key insight is that compressors can be characterized by two parameters (bias and variance), and by designing an algorithm that exploits both error feedback and variance-reduction ideas one can recover DIANA and EF21 as special cases while enabling a broader class of compressors. The proposed method introduces a new algorithm (EF-BV) that operates with this generalized compressor class, combines independent randomness across workers with an error-correction mechanism, and leverages variance reduction to improve convergence as the number of workers grows. The authors prove linear convergence under suitable conditions, showing that EF-BV inherits the practical benefits of biased compressors like top-k and the theoretical scaling advantages of randomized unbiased schemes.

result.text: The paper tackles catastrophic overfitting in single-step adversarial training, a sudden collapse where models become vulnerable to multi-step attacks (PGD) despite appearing robust to single-step attacks (FGSM). The key insight is that using only maximal-perturbation single-step examples concentrates training on boundary points and ignores the continuum of adversarial directions, which distorts the decision boundary and creates a highly curved loss surface that single-step updates cannot reliably defend. The authors analyze this mechanism and propose a simple remedy—augmenting or modifying single-step training to include non-maximal or diversified adversarial examples (thereby sampling the adversarial direction more broadly) to regularize curvature and preserve robustness—showing this prevents catastrophic overfitting and enables single-step procedures to resist multi-step attacks.

result.text: The paper addresses generating counterfactual explanations for graph-level predictions, confronting challenges of discrete graph optimization, generalization to unseen graphs, and preserving causal structure without known causal models. The key insight is to cast counterfactual generation into a generative modeling framework that both smooths the discrete graph search via a latent space and introduces an auxiliary variable to capture causal factors, enabling plausible, causally-aligned perturbations that transfer across graphs. The method, called CLEAR, uses a graph variational autoencoder to encode graphs into a continuous latent space for efficient optimization and generalization, and conditions generation on an auxiliary variable designed to approximate underlying causal influences; counterfactuals are produced by manipulating latent codes and decoding to perturbed graphs that flip the target prediction while remaining realistic and causally coherent. Extensive experiments on synthetic and real-world datasets show CLEAR outperforms prior graph counterfactual methods in validity, sparsity, and causal fidelity.

result.text: The paper addresses the trade-off between pruning accuracy and efficiency: iterative magnitude pruning (IMP) can find high-quality sparse "winning tickets" but is computationally expensive, while faster one-shot methods are efficient but typically produce inferior sparse models. The key insight is to cast pruning as a bi-level optimization (BLO) problem whose specific pruning-retraining structure is bi-linear, which permits reformulating the expensive iterative paradigm into an optimization that admits first-order-style solvers. The authors develop BiP, a BLO-oriented pruning method that leverages this bi-linearity to perform pruning and retraining efficiently, and show theoretically that it can be solved with first-order complexity; empirically BiP finds equal or better winning tickets than IMP across multiple architectures and datasets while matching one-shot methods’ speed, yielding 2–7× speedups over IMP for comparable accuracy and sparsity.

The paper addresses the challenge of designing practical, high-performing active learning algorithms that work with deep neural networks by revisiting Fisher-information–based selection objectives. Its key insight is that bounds on maximum likelihood estimator (MLE) error expressed via the Fisher information can guide selection of informative batches, and that this classic criterion can be made tractable and efficient for neural models by exploiting linear-algebraic structure. The authors propose BAIT, an algorithm that selects batches by optimizing a Fisher-information–based bound on MLE error and implements this optimization with scalable matrix computations suited to modern hardware. Empirically, BAIT consistently outperforms prior active learning methods on both classification and regression tasks and is adaptable to different model architectures.

args.text: We propose a Spectral Multigrid Neural Operator that performs a single transform to the frequency domain and learns a V-cycle entirely in spectral space by partitioning modes into scale bands with resolution-consistent restriction/prolongation defined via Fourier-domain up/down rules. Low-frequency bands parameterize coarse operators for global structure while high-frequency bands learn residual corrections, with inter-band couplings implementing coarse-grid correction; this avoids repeated transforms and balances accuracy–cost. To support irregular meshes, we replace FFTs with efficient direct spectral evaluations while preserving the same banded multigrid algebra. This design inherits multiscale inductive bias and stability from multigrid parameterizations while achieving the runtime and accuracy benefits of transform-once frequency-domain learning and principled spectral upsampling.

result.text: The paper addresses the slow and memory-intensive training of 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) for large-scale scene reconstruction and novel view synthesis. Its key insight is that scene decomposition combined with a distributed consensus optimization—specifically using ADMM—lets multiple local 3DGS models cooperate to learn a single high-quality global model while reducing per-node load and improving convergence stability. Methodologically, DOGS splits a scene into K spatial blocks, runs K local 3DGS trainings on slave nodes that periodically enforce consensus on shared Gaussian parameters with a global model on the master via ADMM, discards the local models after training, and uses only the global model for inference; this yields over 6× faster training on large scenes while maintaining or improving rendering quality.

This yields robust policies with tighter pessimism where needed, reduced over-conservatism on-manifold, and certified lower bounds against adaptive test-time perturbations without online interaction.

result.text: The paper addresses communication bottlenecks in distributed nonconvex optimization by designing gradient compression mechanisms that adapt over training to reduce communication while preserving convergence. The key insight is that allowing compressors to evolve across iterations—captured by a new class called three point compressors (3PC)—unifies and generalizes prior schemes (including EF21) and creates a bridge between error feedback and lazy aggregation, enabling stronger theoretical guarantees without requiring unbiased compressors. result.text: The paper tackles improving neural network pruning beyond standard magnitude-based methods, which decide pruned weights solely by individual magnitude and can be short-sighted when multiple layers interact. The key insight is that magnitude pruning optimizes Frobenius-norm distortion only for a single layer, so extending this objective across multiple consecutive layers—i.e., looking ahead to how pruning in earlier layers affects downstream layers—yields better global fidelity. The authors propose "lookahead pruning," a simple algorithm that jointly selects weights to remove by minimizing multi-layer Frobenius distortion (effectively solving a small multi-layer optimization instead of independent per-layer thresholds) and demonstrate empirically that it consistently outperforms magnitude pruning on architectures like VGG and ResNet, especially at high sparsity.

The paper tackles the scalability and redundancy problems of batch active learning when very large batches are needed, where naive batch selection loses adaptivity and wastes labels on redundant examples. The key insight is that combining uncertainty scoring with an efficient diversity-aware selection procedure lets one retain the benefits of active learning while avoiding intra-batch redundancy even at batch sizes of 100K–1M. Methodologically, the authors propose a scalable sampling algorithm that ranks examples by uncertainty and then selects a diverse subset via fast approximate diversification (with implementation choices that make it computationally tractable at massive scale), empirically demonstrating large improvements over recent baselines and offering an initial theoretical label-complexity analysis for a related, approximately equivalent sampler.

args.text: Adaptive Nonuniform Spectral Operators (ANSO): We propose neural-operator layers that learn a small, continuous set of frequency locations per block and perform global convolution by nonuniform spectral sampling. Concretely, we evaluate the input field’s Fourier transform at the learned k-points via direct nonuniform spectral evaluation, apply learned complex multipliers and low-rank channel mixing in frequency space, and map back with an inverse nonuniform transform; sharing the learned k-point bank across several layers enables a transform-once regime, while optional windowed (local) variants provide spatial adaptivity and reduce over-smoothing. This transfers the idea of learnable sampling positions from deformable/dilated CNNs to the operator’s spectral symbol and extends non-equispaced spectral operators by making the mode set itself learnable. We hypothesize improved accuracy–compute tradeoffs on anisotropic PDEs and irregular meshes (with M≪N learned modes), and ablate shared vs. per-layer banks and local gating.

result.text: The paper tackles the scalability bottleneck of 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) training, which is typically restricted to a single GPU and thus cannot handle high-resolution or large-scale scenes; the key insight is that because each Gaussian only contributes to a small, dynamic subset of pixels, training can be distributed by communicating only the required Gaussians to the corresponding pixel partitions and dynamically balancing load. They implement this idea in Grendel, a distributed system that partitions 3DGS parameters across GPUs, uses sparse all-to-all communication to transfer relevant Gaussians to pixel shards, supports batched multi-view training (rather than one view at a time), and applies a simple sqrt(batch size) hyperparameter scaling rule. By enabling dynamic partitioning and sparse communication, Grendel scales 3DGS to tens of millions of Gaussians across many GPUs and demonstrably improves reconstruction quality on large, high-resolution scenes (e.g., raising PSNR from 26.28 to 27.28 on Rubble by moving from 11.2M Gaussians on one GPU to 40.4M on 16 GPUs).

Its key insight is to introduce equivariant local complete frames—orthonormal bases constructed from node coordinates via cross products—that avoid direction degeneration and let tensor-valued features be projected into a compact, complete local representation. The method embeds these frames into graph neural network layers to process and combine projected tensor information efficiently (since frames are formed using only cross products), yielding an expressive yet computationally light SE(3)-equivariant architecture. Experiments on Newtonian dynamics and molecular conformation generation show the approach matches or outperforms prior equivariant models while being efficient.

result.text: The paper studies why fast single-step adversarial training with FGSM can suddenly fail—“catastrophic overfitting”—losing robustness during training, and questions whether the commonly used random initialization fixes the issue. The key insight is that randomness only helps by shrinking effective perturbation size and that catastrophic overfitting arises from local nonlinearity (even in tiny networks or a single filter) which makes the FGSM linear approximation invalid. To address this, the authors introduce GradAlign, a regularizer that maximizes alignment of input gradients within the perturbation set so the FGSM perturbation better matches multi-step solutions, thereby preventing overfitting and enabling effective fast adversarial training for larger ℓ∞ radii. Experiments show GradAlign narrows the robustness gap to multi-step methods while keeping training efficient.

result.text: The paper addresses efficient training of N:M structured sparsity—where at most N out of every M consecutive weights are nonzero—without costly pretraining or dense-gradient overhead. Its key insight is to view N:M sparsity as a finite combinatorial selection problem over C(M,N) possible N-sized combinations per M-block and to learn which combinations are best via differentiable scores rather than exhaustively searching. The method divides each M-block into all combination subsets, assigns each subset a learnable score that is jointly optimized with its associated weights, and progressively prunes low-scored subsets during standard training, yielding an efficient divide-and-conquer procedure that models relative importance among combinations and outperforms prior N:M pruning approaches.

The paper addresses active learning in realistic, challenging settings—such as class imbalance with rare classes, out-of-distribution (OOD) examples in the unlabeled pool, and redundancy—where standard acquisition strategies fail. The key insight is that submodular information measures (SIM) can capture notions of representativeness, relevance, and diversity in a unified, principled way, allowing acquisition functions to be tailored to different practical issues (e.g., focusing on rare classes or avoiding OOD data) while remaining scalable. The authors propose SIMILAR, an active learning framework that applies various SIM-based acquisition functions to select batches of examples, leveraging submodularity for efficient greedy optimization and extensions that incorporate label priors or query-specific constraints to handle imbalance and OOD. Empirically, SIMILAR consistently outperforms existing methods on image classification benchmarks (CIFAR-10, MNIST, ImageNet), yielding substantial gains especially for rare-class and OOD scenarios, and is released as part of the DISTIL toolkit.

result.text: We propose Anchor-Induced Unbiased EF-BV for federated learning with partial participation and unreliable links. Each round, a small anchor set sends near-uncompressed or induced-unbiased references that define a variance-reduced control variate at the server, while miners transmit highly compressed contractive updates with error-feedback; by transforming miners’ compressors into induced-unbiased ones and analyzing them within the EF-BV framework, the server attains low-bias aggregation and linear convergence under heterogeneity. To handle packet loss and heterogeneous budgets, miners’ compressed updates are encoded with an EDEN-style erasure-robust scheme, and missing contributions are debiased using the anchor reference. An adaptive scheduler tunes anchor frequency and compression levels to trade off bias, variance, and reliability, improving communication and round complexity over pure EF21 or unbiased-only baselines.

result.text: The paper addresses robust overfitting in adversarial training, where networks fit adversarial examples on the training set but generalize poorly to test data, and seeks theoretical generalization guarantees despite the nonsmooth outer maximization defining adversarial loss. The key insight is that although the adversarial (outer) loss is nonsmooth, it satisfies an η-approximate smoothness property with η depending on the perturbation magnitude ε, which lets one extend uniform stability analyses to this setting. Methodologically, the authors prove stability-based generalization bounds for SGD on the class of η-approximate smooth functions (thereby covering adversarial loss), showing that robust test error degrades with ε as training time T grows—between Ω(ε√T) and O(εT)—and they theoretically characterize how practices like early stopping, cyclic learning rates, and stochastic weight averaging improve stability and thus mitigate robust overfitting.

result.text: The paper tackles the problem of open-set active learning, where unlabeled pools contain out-of-distribution (OOD) samples that can degrade standard active learning by causing inefficient or biased sampling. Its key insight is that not all OOD data are harmful—selectively including informative OOD instances alongside in-distribution (ID) samples can simultaneously improve the ID classifier and the OOD detector, whereas exclusively filtering OOD samples can constrain model learning. The authors propose Progressive Active Learning (PAL), a simple progressive sampling scheme that scores unlabeled instances by a combination of informativeness and representativeness and, in each round, balances the selection of pseudo-ID and pseudo-OOD samples to enrich training signals for both tasks; experiments across diverse open-set AL settings show PAL outperforms prior methods.

The paper tackles the problem of high model inconsistency in decentralized federated learning (DFL), which degrades performance under data heterogeneity and sparse communication by causing distribution shift compared to centralized FL. Its key insight is that promoting locally "flat" solutions via Sharpness Aware Minimization (SAM) reduces sensitivity to local variations and, when combined with additional gossip-based mixing, accelerates consensus and mitigates divergence across clients. result.text: The paper addresses the lack of robustness in multi-agent reinforcement learning (MARL), where policies that perform well in training can fail under small environment shifts, noisy observations, or adversarial agent actions. The key insight is that controlling a policy’s Lipschitz constant yields robustness guarantees and that, under mild conditions, there exist Lipschitz policies that remain close to optimal. Building on this, the authors introduce ERNIE, an adversarial-regularization framework that explicitly promotes Lipschitz continuity of policies with respect to states and actions—implemented via adversarial perturbations and stabilized by casting the regularizer as a Stackelberg game—and validate its effectiveness empirically in traffic-light and particle environments while also extending the approach to mean-field MARL through a distributionally robust optimization formulation.

The paper tackles the computational cost of adversarial training, challenging the belief that strong iterative adversaries like PGD are necessary to learn robust deep networks. The key insight is that the cheap fast gradient sign method (FGSM), when paired with random input initialization and standard efficiency tricks, can produce robustness comparable to PGD-based training at a fraction of the cost, provided a specific failure mode is avoided. The authors develop and evaluate FGSM-based adversarial training protocols, demonstrate dramatic speedups (e.g., robust CIFAR-10 and ImageNet classifiers trained in minutes–hours with competitive robust accuracy), and diagnose “catastrophic overfitting” as the reason prior FGSM attempts failed, offering practical recommendations and code to reproduce their results.

result.text: The paper addresses the limitation of common spatial up-sampling operators (interpolation, transposed conv, un-pooling) which rely on local pixel relationships and thus struggle to capture global dependencies for multi-scale modeling. The key insight is that up-sampling can be more globally and theoretically grounded in the Fourier domain via spectral convolution principles, but requires explicit transform rules because Fourier-domain features do not obey local-similarity properties of spatial features. The proposed Deep Fourier Up-Sampling (FourierUp) operator implements this by transforming low-resolution feature maps with a 2D discrete Fourier transform, applying novel Fourier-domain dimension-increase rules to expand spectral representations consistently across resolutions, and mapping back with an inverse 2D Fourier transform; FourierUp is plug-and-play and improves performance across tasks like detection, segmentation, de-raining, dehazing, and guided super-resolution.

result.text: The paper addresses the communication bottleneck in large-scale distributed stochastic gradient descent by improving gossip-based training, whose convergence slows dramatically on large, sparsely connected networks because its rate scales inversely with the spectral gap (1−β). The key insight is that intermittently inserting a periodic global averaging step into Gossip SGD (Gossip-PGA) mitigates the network-topology dependence by using a tunable averaging period H to control the influence of connectivity on transient convergence. Methodologically, Gossip-PGA runs standard local gossip exchanges most iterations but performs a synchronized global model average every H steps, and the authors prove this reduces the transient-stage iteration complexity from Ω(β^4 n^3/(1−β)^4) to Ω(β^4 n^3 H^4) for nonconvex problems—thus trading communication pattern for tunable robustness to poor connectivity—and validate the gains empirically on ResNet50 and BERT.

The paper addresses model-free robust reinforcement learning when the true environment is unknown and the uncertainty set of MDPs must be estimated online from a single misspecified sample trajectory, aiming to optimize worst-case performance without prior knowledge of the uncertainty set. The key insight is that one can estimate the centering misspecified MDP and construct a sample-based uncertainty set incrementally, then plug this estimated set into robust versions of standard RL updates to obtain robustness without requiring extra discount-factor conditions that previous work needed. Methodologically, the authors propose an online robust Q-learning algorithm for the tabular case and a robust TDC algorithm for function approximation, prove convergence (to the optimal robust Q for Q-learning and to stationary points for TDC), derive finite-time error bounds showing convergence rates comparable to non-robust counterparts up to constants, and validate robustness empirically, noting the approach generalizes to other TD-style algorithms.

The paper addresses the approximation gap between random-feature-based attention (RFA) and exact softmax attention in efficient transformer architectures. Its key insight is that RFA can be interpreted as a sum of control-variate estimators—one per sequence element—so that softmax attention can be seen as recoverable by appropriately manipulating these control variates, enabling variance reduction. Building on this view, the authors propose a flexible, learnable control-variate form that yields a novel attention mechanism with substantially reduced approximation error while preserving RFA’s linear time and space complexity, and they validate its effectiveness across vision and language benchmarks.

The paper tackles the problem of reducing communication in distributed stochastic gradient methods while retaining fast convergence when using general (possibly biased) gradient compressors, where naive compression creates persistent errors that slow or break convergence and it was unknown whether error compensation can be combined with Nesterov-style acceleration. The key insight is that error compensation can be incorporated into an accelerated variance-reduced framework in a way that controls the compression error and preserves accelerated linear rates under standard smoothness and strong-convexity assumptions. Concretely, the authors design an error-compensated loopless Katyusha algorithm that maintains and corrects compression residuals while applying the loopless accelerated variance-reduction updates, and they prove an accelerated linear convergence bound for any compressor satisfying a contraction property. Empirically, the method achieves the same optimization accuracy with substantially fewer communication rounds than prior error-compensated algorithms, demonstrating that acceleration and error feedback are compatible in practice.

args.text: Curvature-guided adversarial label transport (C-GALT): We hypothesize that robust overfitting in adversarial training stems from label mismatch induced by adversarial perturbations and local nonlinearity, and propose to assign soft labels to adversarial examples by transporting the clean label distribution along the attack direction using Jacobian–vector products, with a SAM-based curvature probe to modulate transport. Concretely, we generate a one-step adversarial example (e.g., N-FGSM), estimate gradient alignment and a curvature proxy via SAM-style weight perturbations (or lightweight Hessian-norm approximations), and then interpolate the clean one-hot toward the model’s adversarial logits in proportion to misalignment/curvature, yielding per-example adaptive soft labels. This unifies adaptive label smoothing with curvature control to prevent single-step catastrophic overfitting while reducing robust overfitting from label noise, and retains efficiency by reusing quantities already available in fast training. We expect improved robustness–calibration trade-offs and more stable training across larger perturbation radii without extra hyperparameters.

result.text: The paper addresses the lack of large-scale, standardized benchmarks and reproducible evaluation protocols for predicting future links in multi-relational temporal knowledge and heterogeneous graphs, which hampers fair comparison and scalability research. Its key insight is that progress requires both substantially larger, diverse datasets and a unified, realistic evaluation pipeline to reveal practical strengths and limitations of models (e.g., the importance of edge-type information and the competitiveness of simple heuristics). The authors present TGB 2.0, an extension of the Temporal Graph Benchmark that introduces eight new datasets across five domains—some with up to 53 million edges—alongside a reproducible benchmarking framework for temporal link prediction. Experiments using TGB 2.0 demonstrate that many existing methods do not scale to the largest datasets, that exploiting relation types is critical for strong performance, and that research should prioritize scalability and robust baselines.

result.text: The paper addresses the high communication cost in federated learning by eliminating frequent weight updates from clients to server. Its key insight is that useful models can be obtained not by training weights but by learning a sparse subnetwork (a binary mask) within a randomly initialized dense network, so only mask updates—far smaller than full-weight gradients—need to be communicated. The method freezes random initial weights and has clients collaboratively train a stochastic binary mask via federated rounds to identify and converge to an optimal sparse random subnetwork, yielding a final compact model with random weights and a learned sparsity pattern; experiments on MNIST, EMNIST, CIFAR-10 and CIFAR-100 show improved accuracy, faster convergence, and drastic communication reduction (under 1 bit per parameter) compared to baselines in low-bitrate settings.

result.text: The paper addresses the practical deployment problem that Graph Neural Networks (GNNs), while accurate for node classification, incur prohibitive inference latency due to multi-hop neighbor data dependency, making them unsuitable for latency-constrained production settings. The key insight is that multi-layer perceptrons (MLPs) can inherit most of a GNN’s predictive power via knowledge distillation, eliminating graph access at inference while retaining much of the GNN’s accuracy. Their method trains MLPs (termed Graph-less Neural Networks, GLNNs) using distillation from trained GNN teachers across transductive and inductive scenarios, and evaluates trade-offs between accuracy and speed on seven datasets; GLNNs match GNN accuracy on most datasets, improve over standalone MLPs by ~12% on average, and deliver 146–273× faster inference (and 14–27× faster than other acceleration techniques), making them a practical choice for low-latency deployments.

result.text: The paper tackles the gap between linear-attention Transformers—which offer linear-time inference and RNN-style 2D hidden-state formulations—and softmax-attention models, noting that linear attention typically lags in accuracy and existing implementations are I/O-inefficient. The key insight is that by trading off memory movement against parallelizability, one can implement a hardware-efficient linear-attention kernel that outperforms optimized softmax implementations, and that expressivity can be restored by adding data-dependent gating to the linear-attention formulation. The authors introduce FLASHLINEARATTENTION, a fast I/O-aware kernel, and extend it to Gated Linear Attention (GLA) which plugs into Transformers as a drop-in attention replacement; empirically GLA matches or exceeds LLaMA-style and other linear-time baselines on moderate-scale language modeling, generalizes remarkably to much longer contexts (training on 2K, testing >20K) with minimal perplexity loss, and trains faster than comparable linear-time models like Mamba.

FetchSGD addresses the dual challenges in federated learning of heavy communication costs and degraded convergence when client participation is sparse. The key insight is to use a linear, mergeable Count Sketch to compress client model updates so that momentum and error accumulation can be maintained centrally inside the sketch rather than on each client, which preserves state across intermittent clients and enables high compression without losing critical optimization history. Concretely, each client sketches its local gradient/update with a Count Sketch, the server merges these sketches to form an aggregate sketch, performs momentum and error correction in sketch space, and reconstructs sparse updates for model updates; the authors prove convergence guarantees for this procedure and validate it empirically on ResNets and a transformer showing strong communication savings and robust convergence.

args.text: Dual-Perturbation Label-Consistent Adversarial Training (DP-LCAT) jointly perturbs inputs and weights and calibrates labels to mitigate both catastrophic and robust overfitting. For each batch, we (i) create a diversified, noise-seeded single-step adversarial example (non-maximal step plus N-FGSM-style noise), (ii) apply a SAM-style weight perturbation, and (iii) train with a combined loss that enforces prediction consistency across the two perturbations, adds a GradAlign-like gradient alignment term, and uses soft targets whose entropy is set by the example’s adversarial susceptibility (e.g., logit change along the attack direction). This simultaneously smooths input- and weight-space loss, corrects adversarial label mismatch, and improves calibration compared to using any component alone. We hypothesize improved robust accuracy and calibration across perturbation radii at single-step cost, with stability further enhanced via early stopping or SWA schedules.

result.text: The paper addresses the gap between costly post-training pruning and low-performing pruning-at-initialization by studying during-training pruning and why pruned networks often fail to recover accuracy. Its key insight is that "pruning plasticity" — a network’s ability to regain original performance after connections are removed — governs pruning outcomes, and that plasticity can be substantially boosted by neuroregeneration, a brain-inspired mechanism that replaces pruned connections with newly initialized ones. Building on this, the authors propose GraNet, a gradual magnitude pruning algorithm with zero-cost neuroregeneration that regenerates as many connections as are pruned during training, and demonstrate that this approach improves recovery and overall sparse training performance, including a sparse-to-sparse ResNet-50 result on ImageNet that surpasses dense-to-sparse baselines without extra training time.

result.text: The paper addresses communication bottlenecks in federated learning by reducing the cost of transmitting model updates between clients and server while preserving model accuracy. The key insight is that model updates can be compressed effectively by approximating weight matrices as a low-rank factorization modulated elementwise by a small Hadamard-product mask, which captures important fine-grained variations without full-rank transmission. The proposed FedPara method decomposes each layer’s update into two low-rank factors plus a sparse or low-parameter Hadamard mask, transmits only these compact components (and optionally their signs/quantized values), and reconstructs the full update at the server for aggregation; experiments show this yields large communication savings with minimal accuracy loss across federated benchmarks.

result.text: The paper tackles offline reinforcement learning, where the challenge is to learn reliable policies from fixed logged data without environment interaction, focusing on avoiding overoptimistic behavior in regions poorly covered by the dataset. Its key insight is to cast model-based offline RL as a two-player zero-sum game in which an adversarial dynamics model is trained to both fit the dataset and minimize the policy’s estimated value, thereby inducing pessimism where the data is scarce. The method, RAMBO, alternates between policy optimization inside the learned model and adversarial model updates that trade off data likelihood with value minimization, yielding a conservative value estimate that provably lower-bounds true performance under PAC-style guarantees. Empirically, RAMBO achieves stronger and more robust performance than prior state-of-the-art offline RL baselines on standard benchmarks.

result.text: The paper tackles the practical challenge of converting large pretrained Transformer language models into more deployable, efficient linear RNN–based hybrids without sacrificing performance. Its key insight is that attention-layer linear projection weights from Transformers can be reused to distill much of the model’s capacity into a Mamba-style linear RNN, enabling removal of many attention layers while preserving generation quality and even improving length extrapolation. The authors build hybrid models that keep roughly a quarter of the original attention layers and replace the rest with linear RNN components via distillation from Llama3-8B-Instruct, demonstrate superior chat and general-benchmark performance compared to scratch-trained hybrids, and introduce a hardware-aware speculative decoding algorithm to speed inference of Mamba and hybrid models. Overall, with academic GPU resources they open-source distilled checkpoints and show strong wins on AlpacaEval 2 and MT-Bench plus near-perfect long-context needle-in-a-haystack accuracy at 20× distillation length.

result.text: The paper addresses the challenge of learning interpretable logical rules for reasoning over temporal knowledge graphs (tKGs), where facts evolve over time and temporal complexity hampers accurate link prediction. The key insight is that incorporating temporal operators and explicit temporal features (recurrence, order, inter-relation intervals, duration) into a differentiable rule-learning framework lets the model capture temporal patterns while remaining interpretable and trainable end-to-end. The proposed method, TILP, implements a constrained random-walk mechanism augmented with temporal operators to efficiently search and score candidate temporal rules, integrates temporal feature modeling into the learning objective, and is trained differentiably to optimize rule weights; experiments on two benchmarks show improved performance and robustness under limited, biased, or temporally shifted training data compared to state-of-the-art baselines.

The paper tackles efficient, symmetry-preserving prediction of quantum Hamiltonian matrices for molecular systems, where maintaining SE(3) equivariance typically conflicts with computational and memory efficiency. The key insight is an architectural design that enforces SE(3)-equivariance while drastically reducing costly tensor-product operations and preventing exponential channel growth as atom types increase. The authors propose QHNet, an SE(3)-equivariant graph neural network that restructures equivariant message passing to cut tensor products by 92%, streamlines channels to limit dimensional blowup, and uses this lightweight equivariant circuitry to predict Hamiltonian entries. On four MD17 molecular datasets QHNet matches state-of-the-art accuracy with much faster runtimes and about 50% lower memory consumption.

result.text: The paper addresses the limitation of Sharpness-Aware Minimization (SAM), observing that minimizing the perturbed-loss (maximum loss in a neighborhood) does not necessarily prefer flat minima because different curvature directions can yield similarly low perturbed loss. The key insight is to introduce the "surrogate gap," a computable quantity that, for small neighborhood radii, is equivalent to the dominant Hessian eigenvalue at a minimum and therefore directly measures sharpness; minimizing this gap together with the perturbed loss targets regions that are both low-loss and low-sharpness. The proposed method, GSAM, augments SAM with an inexpensive two-step routine—(1) a SAM-like descent to reduce perturbed loss and (2) an ascent (i.e., corrective) step in the gradient-orthogonal direction to explicitly reduce the surrogate gap—yielding provable convergence and improved generalization empirically (notably +3.2% over SAM on ImageNet for ViT-B/32).

result.text: The paper addresses the challenge of finding compact, high-performing sparse neural networks without the costly multi-stage pipeline of traditional pruning methods. Its key insight is to jointly learn both network weights and a trainable, layer-wise pruning threshold via backpropagation so that the sparse structure is adapted dynamically during standard training rather than imposed afterward. The method introduces masked layers with learnable thresholds that push small-magnitude activations/weights to zero and are optimized alongside weights, enabling the model to reach high sparsity with little performance loss in the same number of epochs as dense training. Empirical results show competitive or superior sparsity–accuracy tradeoffs across architectures and reveal that dynamic, fine-grained thresholding exposes limitations of three-stage pruning and offers guidance for designing inherently compact networks.

The paper addresses reducing uplink communication in federated learning under realistic challenges—partial client participation and heterogeneous data—while handling the distortion introduced by communication compression. Its key insight is that the classical stochastic controlled averaging (SCA) can be reformulated into an equivalent but simpler and more communication-efficient implementation that halves uplink cost and serves as a foundation for compression-aware algorithms. Building on that reformulation, the authors develop two algorithms—SCALLION for unbiased compressors and SCAFCOM for biased compressors—that integrate compressed updates without extra assumptions on compression error or limits on heterogeneity, and they prove improved communication and computation complexity relative to prior work. Empirically, both methods match full-precision FL performance with much less uplink transmission and beat recent compressed-FL baselines under the same communication budget.

The paper addresses the prohibitive per-decision computation cost of sequential Bayesian optimal experimental design, which prevents real-time adaptive experiments in many practical settings. Its key insight is that the sequential design problem can be amortized by learning a policy network that maps past observations to the next experimental design, so decisions during deployment require only a single forward pass. The method trains this amortized design network using newly proposed contrastive information bounds as objectives tailored to the sequential setting and a symmetry-exploiting neural architecture, and at test time the learned policy produces near-optimal adaptive designs in milliseconds, outperforming baseline strategies across several tasks.

The paper tackles reconstructing and real-time rendering of complex dynamic 3D scenes from 2D images by addressing limitations of neural implicit methods that struggle to capture spatio-temporal structure and to scale deformation modeling. The key insight is to treat spacetime as a single 4D volume and approximate it with explicit, learnable 4D primitives—anisotropic, rotatable 4D Gaussians that carry geometry and view-/time-varying appearance via 4D spheroidal harmonic coefficients—thereby avoiding complex deformation fields and directly encoding spatio-temporal structure. The method optimizes a collection of these 4D Gaussians end-to-end to fit input video frames, and uses a tailored splatting-style renderer to synthesize novel views at any time in real time; experiments show improved visual quality and efficiency across monocular and multi-view dynamic benchmarks.

result.text: The paper addresses the gap in intuition for why Transformer Attention works so well by relating it to a principled associative memory model; specifically, it asks whether and how Attention implements retrieval dynamics similar to Kanerva’s Sparse Distributed Memory (SDM). The key insight is that under realistic data conditions—high-dimensional, approximately isotropic key representations with sparse, distributed activations—dot-product attention closely approximates SDM’s nearest-neighbor, pseudo-random addressing and additive retrieval, so Attention can be seen as performing associative memory readouts rather than just learned weighting. Methodologically, the authors formalize a mapping between the softmax-weighted dot-product attention and SDM’s fixed random address-response scheme, empirically verify that pre-trained GPT-2’s key/query statistics satisfy the required conditions, and analyze the consequences for computational interpretation and biological plausibility of Attention.

The paper tackles the challenge of representing temporal knowledge graphs, which require modeling both static patterns at specific timestamps and dynamic patterns across time, and argues that single-space embeddings are geometrically limited in capturing this variety. Its key insight is that different geometric subspaces (Complex, Dual, and Split-complex) naturally capture different relational and temporal behaviors, so combining them in a product space allows richer, more flexible pattern modeling than any single geometry. The method, HGE, embeds temporal facts into a product space composed of these heterogeneous subspaces and uses a temporal-geometric attention mechanism to weight and integrate information from each subspace based on the relation and timestamp, yielding improved inference performance on standard temporal KG benchmarks.

result.text: The paper addresses how to build neural networks that exactly respect symmetry under any finite-dimensional representation of a reductive Lie group, a need that arises in physics, chemistry, and geometry where data transform under groups like O(n), U(n) or the Lorentz group. The key insight is that the equivariant architectures (generalizing ACE/MACE from atomistic point clouds) can be made fully general by composing learnable maps that operate on tensors decomposed into irreducible representations and by using algebraic routines to reduce arbitrary tensor products, ensuring equivariance by construction. The method implements this idea as a modular network design plus the lie-nn software library, which automates tensor-product decomposition and projection into irreducibles so practitioners can assemble G‑equivariant layers for any reductive Lie group; the approach is validated on Lorentz-group-based top-quark tagging and orthogonal-group shape recognition tasks.

The paper tackles the bottleneck in decentralized federated learning where synchronous model exchanges force all clients to wait for the slowest participant, slowing wall-clock convergence and increasing communication overhead. The key insight is that a wait-free, asynchronous communication protocol can let clients train and share updates at their own pace while still preserving the theoretical iteration-wise convergence rate of parallel SGD and avoiding bounded-delay assumptions. The proposed method, SWIFT, implements a decentralized wait-free model/gradient exchange scheme with provable O(1/√T) convergence for convex and nonconvex smooth problems under IID and non-IID data, and shows empirically that eliminating synchronization dramatically reduces per-epoch communication time and yields substantially faster wall-clock convergence (up to ~50% faster to given loss) than synchronous and other asynchronous baselines.

The paper addresses the problem of providing formal robustness guarantees for reinforcement learning policies against adversarial perturbations, both in terms of per-state action stability and worst-case cumulative reward. The key insight is that smoothing techniques applied to value-based policies can certify action invariance and lower bounds on finite-horizon returns: local smoothing around states yields protections for individual actions along a trajectory, while global smoothing (and an adaptive local search variant) can produce tight certified lower bounds on cumulative rewards. The method, called CROP, instantiates these ideas for policies derived from Q-functions by developing a local smoothing algorithm to guarantee action robustness, a global smoothing algorithm to certify finite-horizon reward bounds, and an adaptive local smoothing search to tighten reward certificates, and it empirically evaluates these certificates (and their tightness) across several robust RL training methods and four environments.

result.text: The paper addresses understanding and improving linearized self-attention by connecting it to Fast Weight Programmers (FWPs), i.e., systems where a slow network programs a fast memory via additive outer-product updates, and identifies capacity and adaptability limitations in recent linear attention variants. Its key insight is that linearized attention is formally equivalent to classic outer-product FWPs, which suggests replacing purely additive programming instructions with delta-rule-like updates and learned, dynamic learning rates so the fast memory can correct and adapt mappings from keys to values. Methodologically, the authors derive this equivalence, analyze memory capacity, introduce a delta-rule-inspired update and a new kernel for linearizing attention, and validate the approach on synthetic retrieval tasks, machine translation, and language modeling, showing improved adaptability and performance.

The paper tackles the problem of distributed mean estimation (DME) in federated learning under heterogeneous client communication budgets and packet losses, which cause increased estimation error when gradients are lossy-compressed. The key insight is to design a compression-and-aggregation scheme that is inherently robust to differing per-client budgets and unreliable delivery, so that the server can recover an accurate global mean despite missing or differently-compressed contributions. The proposed method, EDEN, combines tailored stochastic compression operators with an encoding/decoding protocol and theoretical bias/variance analysis that account for budget heterogeneity and packet drop probabilities, yielding provable error bounds; empirical evaluations show EDEN consistently outperforms prior DME techniques in both accuracy and communication efficiency.

result.text: The paper addresses why adversarial training suffers from robust overfitting and its puzzling dependence on perturbation radius and data quality by identifying a previously overlooked source of error: label noise. The key insight is that adversarial perturbations distort the true label distribution of examples, so inheriting the original clean labels for adversarial counterparts introduces label noise that fuels overfitting and explains epoch-wise double descent. Methodologically, the authors analyze this label-mismatch theoretically and empirically and propose an automatic label-calibration scheme that adjusts labels for adversarial examples to counteract the noise, yielding consistent robustness improvements across models and datasets without extra hyperparameters or tuning.

result.text: The paper tackles latent graph inference for tasks where the true connectivity is unknown or suboptimal by extending the Differentiable Graph Module (dDGM) to richer geometric embedding spaces. The key insight is that using product manifolds of constant-curvature Riemannian model spaces (and learning their curvatures) yields latent representations that capture heterogeneous relational structure better than a single Euclidean plane, enabling more informative similarity measures for graph construction. Methodologically, the authors design a tractable way to embed node features onto learned product manifolds, compute similarity-based edge probabilities in that geometry, and train curvature parameters jointly with the network end-to-end; empirical results across diverse datasets show consistent improvements over the original Euclidean dDGM.

result.text: The paper tackles certifying neural network robustness to patch adversarial attacks—localized perturbations confined to a bounded image region—by providing guarantees that no adversarial patch can change a classifier’s decision for a given image and patch size. The key insight is that patch attacks are far more constrained than arbitrary sparse perturbations, so randomized smoothing techniques can be adapted and de-randomized to yield large, deterministic robustness certificates rather than just high-confidence probabilistic ones. Methodologically, the authors develop a de-randomized smoothing algorithm tailored to patches that computes deterministic certificates and can be applied to standard classifiers without expensive specialized training; this approach scales to CIFAR-10 and ImageNet and empirically outperforms the prior interval-bound-propagation baseline, achieving much higher certified and clean accuracies for practical patch sizes.

The paper addresses the problem of reducing downlink communication in cross-device federated learning, where clients are often heterogeneous and may participate only once so they must download full model parameters (making typical uplink-oriented, decaying-update compressors ineffective). The key insight is that downlink compression can be made practical by designing a framework that accounts for one-shot client appearances and can be combined with uplink schemes to enable bi-directional compression without hurting model accuracy. DoCoFL implements this idea by applying tailored compression mechanisms on server-to-client transmissions (compatible with a variety of uplink compressors), and demonstrates through extensive experiments that it substantially reduces total bandwidth in both directions while maintaining accuracy close to an uncompressed baseline.

result.text: The paper addresses generative modeling of crystalline materials to both predict stable crystal structures for known compositions and propose new compositions with realizable structures, a challenge made difficult by the extreme sparsity of thermodynamically stable arrangements and the complex symmetries of periodic lattices. result.text: The paper tackles the challenge of efficiently finding optimal sequential experimental designs under Bayesian criteria, where traditional Bayesian solutions are computationally expensive and recent amortized policies can fail to explore well, require differentiable models, and are limited to continuous designs. Its key insight is that optimizing a policy for sequential design can be framed exactly as a Markov decision process, enabling the use of reinforcement learning to learn exploration-aware, model-agnostic design strategies. The authors therefore train parameterized policies with modern deep RL methods to solve the MDP, which yields a deployment-efficient sampler that performs well on both continuous and discrete design spaces and works with black-box probabilistic models.

args.text: WF-Moshpit OT-Consensus brings fully decentralized, wait-free fusion to distributed 3D Gaussian Splatting by first matching co-visible Gaussians via lightweight, visibility-aware entropic OT and then running identity-agnostic Moshpit-style iterative averaging on the matched sets. Shards asynchronously exchange only overlapping blocks, solve tiny OT problems to obtain soft correspondences, and push/average sufficient statistics (means, covariances, SH) with uncertainty/opacity weights, while spawning/pruning unmatched mass locally to avoid brittle parameter equality. The moshpit mixing yields exponential convergence of matched subsets under intermittent connectivity and stragglers, eliminating masters and global sync while keeping bandwidth comparable to sparse all-to-all; empirically this should reduce duplication/oscillation and improve large-scene PSNR/LPIPS over ADMM or posterior-averaging baselines. result.text: The paper addresses certifying provable adversarial robustness for reinforcement learning agents under adaptive attackers who can tailor perturbations across time by observing past states and actions, a setting where prior per-timestep static defenses are insufficient. Its key insight is an adaptive extension of randomized smoothing theory—specifically an adaptive Neyman-Pearson lemma—that allows certification of the total cumulative reward rather than requiring the policy to be robust at every intermediate step, thereby accounting for attackers whose perturbations can depend stochastically on past observations and actions. Methodologically, the authors propose "policy smoothing," which injects Gaussian noise into observations before feeding them to the policy, derive tight certificates that lower-bound the final total reward under any adaptive attack (and construct matching worst-case attacks to show tightness), and validate the approach empirically on control and Atari-like environments to demonstrate meaningful practical guarantees.

result.text: The paper addresses few-shot temporal knowledge graph reasoning: predicting future facts for newly emerging entities in evolving temporal knowledge graphs where only very limited historical observations exist and distributions may shift over time. The key insight is that rigid, one-size-fits-all neighbor sampling and aggregation fails under both data scarcity and temporal drift, so the model should learn to dynamically adapt how it selects and pools recent contextual facts for each new entity using feedback from future facts. The paper addresses supervised learning for predicting properties of crystalline materials, noting that standard graph neural networks used for molecules fail to exploit the richer symmetry structure of crystals. result.text: The paper addresses the dual challenges in federated learning of high communication overhead from frequent server–client synchronization and the limited adaptivity of SGD-based updates, noting that existing approaches (compression or adaptive optimizers) do not jointly resolve both issues. The key insight is that communication-efficient compression can be integrated with adaptive optimization in a principled way that preserves convergence guarantees: by designing compressors and adaptive update rules that control the additional variance and bias introduced by compression, one can retain the same nonconvex stochastic convergence rate as uncompressed adaptive methods. The method, FedCAMS, combines momentum/second-moment style adaptive updates with tailored communication compression and server–client aggregation rules, and the authors prove FedCAMS achieves O(1/√(T K m)) convergence in the nonconvex setting while validating its empirical performance across benchmarks.

The paper addresses the problem of performing Bayesian optimal experimental design (BOED) adaptively in real time for implicit simulation models that lack tractable likelihoods, where traditional BOED is too computationally expensive to run during experiments. The key insight is to amortize experiment-time cost by training a design policy network offline that learns to map current data and context to near-optimal next-design decisions, enabling millisecond-scale deployment without requiring closed-form likelihoods or conditional independence. The method, called implicit Deep Adaptive Design (iDAD), trains the policy on simulated differentiable samples from the model using objectives that capture expected information gain (or related utilities) and then applies the learned policy online to select experimental settings rapidly. Empirical results demonstrate that iDAD yields fast, effective adaptive designs across multiple tasks, extending policy-based BOED to a much broader class of implicit models.

The paper tackles limitations in prompt learning for vision-language models, specifically that existing trainable prompts are derived from global image features and treated equally, which can ignore discriminative foreground details and fail under distribution shift. Its key insight is that prompts should be grounded in local, spatially localized image features and adaptively weighted according to image-specific semantics, yielding dynamic prompts aligned with relevant regions and local contextual relationships. The proposed Contextual Prompt Learning (CoPL) framework incorporates local image features into prompt construction and learns an attention-like weighting mechanism to reweight and align multiple prompts to task-relevant local features, producing region-aware, dynamically composed prompts. Experiments on standard, few-shot, and out-of-distribution benchmarks demonstrate substantially improved generalization and robustness compared to prior prompt-learning approaches.

result.text: We propose a compute-aware co-active learning framework that jointly selects labeled batches and a sparse parameter-update mask to maximize expected generalization gain per unit wall-clock and communication budget. Concretely, we optimize a Fisher-information–based MLE error-reduction bound restricted to a k-parameter mask (linearized/NTK regime), operationalized by alternating steps: (i) pick a fixed mask via top-k Fisher/gradient scores; (ii) choose a large, diversity-regularized batch that maximizes the restricted Fisher gain using scalable matrix sketches. This unifies Fisher-guided selection with massive-batch diversification and fixed-Fisher sparse updating, and extends naturally to streaming by maintaining a sliding-window mask and querying points whose restricted Fisher contributions cross an adaptive threshold. We hypothesize superior label efficiency under tight compute/communication budgets and propose submodular surrogates for the restricted Fisher gain to enable greedy selection with approximation guarantees.

result.text: The paper addresses the problem of limited effective context length in transformer models augmented with key–value external memory, where as memory grows the model is distracted by many irrelevant or overlapping keys (the “distraction issue”), reducing retrieval precision. The key insight is that contrastive-style training can restructure the key space so semantically similar keys are clustered and dissimilar or confusable keys are pushed apart, making it easier for attention to focus on truly relevant memory entries even when the number of keys is large. The method, called Focused Transformer (FoT), fine-tunes existing large models by adding contrastive objectives over (key, value) pairs during training to encourage discriminative key representations, and demonstrates this by fine-tuning 3B and 7B OpenLLaMA models into LongLLaMA variants that show improved long-context performance and handling of contexts up to 256k tokens for retrieval tasks.

The paper tackles the challenge of applying Bayesian optimization to discrete, high-dimensional biological sequence and molecule design problems, where standard BayesOpt struggles because decision variables are not continuous. The key insight is to learn a continuous latent representation with a denoising autoencoder jointly trained with a multi-task Gaussian process predictor, enabling gradient-based optimization of acquisition functions in latent space that can handle multiple objectives and balance exploration–exploitation. Their method, LaMBO, jointly optimizes the autoencoder and GP head so acquisition functions (including multi-objective Pareto-aware variants) can be optimized by gradient descent in latent space, then decoded to discrete sequences; this approach is evaluated on small-molecule and fluorescent-protein design tasks and outperforms genetic optimizers without requiring large pretraining corpora.

Sharpness-Conditioned Adversarial Label Smoothing (SCALS): We hypothesize that robust overfitting arises from label mismatch that is amplified when the local loss landscape is sharp along the adversarial direction. During adversarial training, we estimate per-example sharpness via the GSAM surrogate gap (or a one-step SAM proxy) projected onto the FGSM/N-FGSM perturbation direction, and adaptively calibrate the adversarial label by increasing label smoothing or transporting probability mass toward confusing classes in proportion to this directional sharpness. This combines N-FGSM’s stable single-step generation with curvature-aware label adjustment, aiming to reduce robust overfitting and improve calibration without extra inner-loop steps. We predict SCALS yields better robust test accuracy and ECE than vanilla AT and prior adaptive smoothing baselines across radii and datasets.

result.text: OT-Consensus 3DGS aligns and fuses overlapping local Gaussian sets to a global model via visibility-aware optimal transport (OT), avoiding brittle parameter-wise equality assumptions that break under cloning/splitting and heterogeneous partitions. args.text: We propose Budget-Aware Trajectory Smoothing for Certified Conservative Offline RL (BATS-CORL), which targets certified robustness against adaptive observation attacks constrained by a global L2 budget while avoiding excessive pessimism. Instead of a fixed per-step smoothing, BATS-CORL solves a trajectory-level allocation problem that distributes smoothing radii across states via dynamic programming/convex duality to maximize a differentiable certified return lower bound under a total adversary budget. Training optimizes this certificate jointly with CQL-style value pessimism and neighborhood regularization as in RORL, scaling conservatism by the locally allocated budget so that scarce-budget segments receive tighter protection while dense on-manifold regions remain less conservative. Each client emits a progressive stream: an induced-unbiased coarse core plus successive-refinement bitplanes protected by rateless erasure codes; the server aggregates whatever prefix arrives with an EDEN-style decoder and models truncation within the EF-BV bias–variance lens, pushing unrecovered refinement into error feedback. The scheme adapts its effective rate on-the-fly without per-round retuning, supports time-varying compressors in the spirit of 3PC, and admits linear convergence under PL with error that scales to actually delivered bits rather than nominal budgets. result.text: The paper studies why deep networks that benignly overfit—achieving zero training error even with label noise while generalizing on natural test data—remain vulnerable to adversarial attacks, asking whether bad labels or training dynamics cause this fragility. The key insight is that label noise is a contributor to adversarial vulnerability (robust training sometimes fails to fit noisy labels), but removing noisy labels alone does not restore robustness because standard training biases networks toward “simple” decision boundaries that are easier to fool. The authors empirically identify label noise in common datasets (MNIST, CIFAR), show that adversarial training yields more complex boundaries, and argue theoretically via toy examples that the learned representation critically determines how complex a classifier must be to be robust. Overall, they suggest that both noisy data and suboptimal representation learning interact to produce benign overfitting that is not benign with respect to adversarial robustness.

result.text: The paper addresses loss of plasticity in continual learning—where networks become harder to train as new tasks arrive—by aiming to preserve trainability while retaining performance. The key insight is that the singular value spectrum of layer weight matrices at initialization, particularly keeping the largest singular value near one, is critical for early-phase trainability and that maintaining this property throughout training sustains gradient diversity and plasticity. The authors propose a spectral regularizer that penalizes deviations of each layer’s maximum singular value from one, integrating this term into continual supervised and reinforcement learning training so that weights remain well-conditioned; experiments show this approach preserves trainability, is robust to hyperparameters, improves per-task training, and yields better generalization across architectures and tasks.

The key insight is that a fixed mask selecting the parameters with the largest Fisher information provides a simple, effective proxy for which weights matter most for the task, so those parameters can be the only ones updated repeatedly. result.text: The paper addresses Bayesian optimization for expensive black-box functions with discrete or mixed (discrete+continuous) inputs, where maximizing acquisition functions is hard because gradients are unavailable and exhaustive search is infeasible. result.text: The paper addresses catastrophic forgetting in fake audio detection, where models fine-tuned on a new dataset lose performance on previously learned datasets due to ignoring cross-dataset similarities of genuine audio. The key insight is that weight updates should be adapted based on the relative proportions of genuine versus fake utterances and constrained to preserve the old genuine-audio distribution, rather than applying uniform orthogonal modifications. result.text: The paper addresses the problem of completing temporal knowledge graphs by predicting missing future facts, noting that many relations exhibit repeated patterns over time that standard time-aware embedding methods do not explicitly exploit. The key insight is that temporal prediction can be improved by combining generation from the global entity vocabulary with a time-aware copying mechanism that directly references historically observed facts when repetition is likely. The authors introduce CyGNet, a sequential copy-generation network that models entity and time dynamics and learns a switching mechanism to either copy past fact objects (when repetition is detected) or generate new objects from the full vocabulary, and they evaluate it on five benchmarks showing improved performance on both repetitive and novel fact prediction.

The paper addresses the problem of learning probability distributions defined on manifolds while respecting the intrinsic symmetries (group actions) those manifolds admit, a requirement common in scientific domains like physics but often ignored by existing models. Its key insight is that one can build invertible generative maps (flows) on manifolds that are equivariant with respect to the relevant symmetry group, which ensures the induced densities are symmetry-invariant and that the flow structure is compatible with manifold geometry. Methodologically, the authors develop the theoretical foundations for equivariant manifold flows—constructing equivariant diffeomorphisms and change-of-variable formulas tailored to arbitrary manifolds and group actions—and demonstrate the approach by training gauge-invariant flows to model densities over SU(n) for quantum field theory tasks.

args.text: We propose HATS, a during-training, hardware-aware structured pruning method that preserves trainability while meeting a target latency. HATS alternates an augmented-Lagrangian mask update that selects channels/heads and optional N:M blocks using a calibrated latency table with a trainability-restoration step that combines zero-cost neuroregeneration of pruned connections, spectral-norm regularization to keep per-layer top singular values near one, and Gram-decoupling to reduce harmful parameter correlations. Regenerated weights are sampled to respect the chosen structure and are steered with a lightweight blockwise output-reconstruction loss to limit functional drift during pruning. Compared to post-training pipelines, HATS delivers true wall-clock speedups without brittle recovery, improving sparse-to-sparse training of ViTs/LLMs under strict latency targets.

result.text: We propose Fed-CoBAIT-Mask, a federated compute-aware active learning framework that co-optimizes client selection, label acquisition, and a fixed top-k Fisher update mask to maximize Fisher-based MLE error reduction per transmitted bit and per compute second. Clients maintain low-rank sketches of their local empirical Fisher over a moving window and score unlabeled points by restricted Fisher gain under the mask; the server aggregates these sketches with a compression-aware SCA-style protocol and greedily schedules client/query pairs by marginal gain over communication cost. Model updates are communicated as low-rank-plus-Hadamard masked factors, while optionally training a learned sparse subnetwork to further reduce memory and uplink, yielding label-, compute-, and communication-efficient learning under heterogeneity and partial participation. We further introduce submodular surrogates for the restricted Fisher gain to enable near-optimal greedy selection, and leverage convergence guarantees from compression-aware federated optimization.

result.text: This paper addresses the problem of certifying robustness of offline reinforcement learning against training-time poisoning attacks, where an adversary can arbitrarily manipulate a subset of training trajectories. The key insight is that by defining tractable certification criteria tailored to RL—per-state action stability and cumulative reward bounds—and by using aggregation and partitioning protocols over trajectories, one can provably bound how many poisoned trajectories a learned policy can tolerate. The authors introduce COPA, a certification framework that computes these bounds, proposes temporal and other aggregation schemes to improve robustness, and analyzes the computational limits (showing some certification variants are tight while others are NP-complete). Empirical results across algorithms and environments show the proposed aggregation methods substantially boost certified robustness and that certification tightness and tolerable poisoning vary by algorithm and environment.

result.text: We propose Rateless Progressive EF-BV for federated/distributed SGD over unreliable links and heterogeneous client budgets. Each client emits a progressive stream: an induced-unbiased coarse core plus successive-refinement bitplanes protected by rateless erasure codes; the server aggregates whatever prefix arrives with an EDEN-style decoder and models truncation within the EF-BV bias–variance lens, pushing unrecovered refinement into error feedback. The scheme adapts its effective rate on-the-fly without per-round retuning, supports time-varying compressors in the spirit of 3PC, and admits linear convergence under PL with error that scales to actually delivered bits rather than nominal budgets. We predict superior accuracy–latency tradeoffs versus fixed-rate Top-K/EF21 or unbiased-only baselines in high drop-rate, heterogeneous-participation regimes.

result.text: The paper addresses the problem of robust overfitting in adversarial training, where models trained with strong adversaries lose robustness after prolonged training and the causes remain unclear. The key insight is that weak adversaries generate mostly small-loss adversarial examples while strong adversaries produce a diverse mix including many large-loss examples, and that some small-loss examples in strong-adversary training are “unworthy” and drive overfitting by being overly easy to fit. To mitigate this, the authors propose Minimum Loss Constrained Adversarial Training (MLCAT), which in each minibatch continues to train on large-loss examples but deliberately prevents overfitting to small-loss examples by increasing their loss (hindering their fitting), with two practical algorithmic implementations. Experiments show MLCAT eliminates robust overfitting and improves adversarial robustness across settings.

result.text: The paper addresses the limitation of neural network-based wave functions that can only model different geometries of the same fixed set of atoms, preventing a single model from generalizing across molecules with different compositions. The key insight is to learn transferable local electronic representations via graph-based message passing that connect molecular orbitals to covalent bonds, enabling embeddings that capture local electronic structure common to multiple molecules. The authors introduce Globe, a graph-learned orbital embedding scheme, and Moon, a size-consistent molecular orbital network Ansatz that uses those embeddings to jointly solve Schrödinger equations for different molecules; empirically Moon converges about 4.5× faster to comparable or lower energies and yields additive energy scaling with system size where prior methods diverged. Together, Globe and Moon demonstrate for the first time that a single neural wave function can generalize across molecules with different atoms.

result.text: The paper tackles the challenge of offline reinforcement learning where standard off-policy methods overestimate action values due to distributional shift between a static dataset and the learned policy, causing poor performance especially on complex, multi-modal data. The key insight is to learn a conservative Q-function that intentionally underestimates values for out-of-distribution actions so that the Q-estimate lower-bounds the true policy value, preventing spurious optimistic updates. Methodologically, Conservative Q-Learning (CQL) adds a simple Q-value regularizer to the Bellman error objective that penalizes Q-values of actions sampled from a broad set (e.g., policy and dataset actions) while preserving accuracy on dataset actions; this regularizer can be implemented on top of existing deep Q-learning or actor-critic algorithms and is shown theoretically to produce a value lower bound and empirically to yield substantially better returns across discrete and continuous benchmarks.

result.text: We propose Loss- and Participation-Aware Bias–Variance Compression (LP-BVC) for federated/distributed SGD with partial client participation and unreliable links. Using the EF-BV framework, each client adaptively selects a compressor along the bias–variance frontier (e.g., switching between EF21-style error-feedback and induced-unbiased transforms) to minimize a per-round surrogate of convergence error that accounts for its local gradient variance, participation probability, and drop rate. The server aggregates via an EDEN-like decoding that is robust to heterogeneous budgets and packet loss, and maintains control-variate statistics to stabilize the adaptively changing compressors across rounds. We hypothesize linear convergence under PL and improved communication/sample complexity versus fixed-compressor baselines in lossy, sparse-participation regimes, and provide a practical policy (a one-step lookahead minimizing predicted MSE of the global update) for compressor selection.
