result.text: The paper addresses why modern structured state-space models (SSMs) with multiplicative input–state interactions (selectivity) outperform attention-based models on sequence tasks. The key insight is that selective linear recurrences transform the input stream so the hidden state becomes a low-dimensional projection of the input’s signature from Rough Path Theory, a mathematical object that compactly encodes non‑linear, multi-timescale interactions among tokens. The authors show theoretically that random linear recurrences with simple input-controlled transitions provably capture signature information, which explains the empirical power of architectures like Mamba and provides a principled framework for assessing and designing future selective SSM variants.

We propose Anchor-Induced Unbiased EF-BV for federated learning with partial participation and unreliable links. Each round, a small anchor set sends near-uncompressed or induced-unbiased references that define a variance-reduced control variate at the server, while miners transmit highly compressed contractive updates with error-feedback; by transforming miners’ compressors into induced-unbiased ones and analyzing them within the EF-BV framework, the server attains low-bias aggregation and linear convergence under heterogeneity. To handle packet loss and heterogeneous budgets, miners’ compressed updates are encoded with an EDEN-style erasure-robust scheme, and missing contributions are debiased using the anchor reference. An adaptive scheduler tunes anchor frequency and compression levels to trade off bias, variance, and reliability, improving communication and round complexity over pure EF21 or unbiased-only baselines.

result.text: The paper addresses communication- and sample-efficient federated learning for a class of nonconvex minimax problems that arise in applications like adversarial training and AUROC maximization, where existing algorithms are largely developed for centralized settings and do not scale well across clients. The key insight is that careful design of federated stochastic gradient-descent-ascent variants with momentum and periodic communication can close the gap between federated and single-machine complexities for common minimax structures (nonconvex-concave, nonconvex-strongly-concave, and nonconvex-PL). The authors propose two algorithms, FedSGDA+ for nonconvex-concave problems and FedSGDA-M for nonconvex-strongly-concave/PL problems, and prove reduced communication complexity O(ε^{-6}) for the former and matching-best sample complexity O(κ^3 N^{-1} ε^{-3}) plus best-known communication complexity O(κ^2 ε^{-2}) for the latter, with experiments on fair classification and AUROC maximization validating their efficiency.

The paper addresses how to choose what an agent should learn when optimal policy synthesis is infeasible due to complexity or resource constraints, formalizing the trade-off between information acquisition and policy sub-optimality. Its key insight is to cast the designer's preference over this trade-off as a single rate-distortion hyperparameter and use rate-distortion theory to let the agent autonomously compute learning targets that optimally balance information cost against performance loss. The method derives a principled optimization for target policies under an information constraint, proves a general expected discounted regret bound for agents that decide what to learn in this way, and demonstrates via computational experiments that this approach can flexibly express designer preferences and in some cases outperform baselines like Thompson sampling in finding optimal policies.

result.text: The paper addresses the limited and uneven memory capacity of modern Hopfield networks, where retrieval dynamics can get stuck in many metastable states causing memory confusion. Its key insight is that a learnable feature map Φ can kernelize the Hopfield energy so that fixed points of retrieval align with local minima in kernel space, and that enforcing separation of stored patterns in this space yields a kernel-induced similarity that spreads local minima more uniformly. Methodologically, the authors introduce U-Hop, a two-stage retrieval procedure that first trains Φ via a separation loss LΦ to distribute local minima (Stage I) and then runs standard Hopfield energy minimization in the transformed space for retrieval (Stage II), empirically demonstrating reduced metastability and improved associative-memory and downstream performance compared to prior Hopfield models and similarity measures.

The paper addresses the communication bottleneck in distributed stochastic optimization caused by contractive (biased) compressors like Top-K, for which the standard remedy—error feedback (EF)—has limitations in theory and practice. The key insight is that any contractive compressor can be transformed into an induced unbiased compressor, enabling the use of the richer set of algorithms and analyses available for unbiased compression rather than relying on EF. Methodologically, the authors construct a transformation that produces an unbiased compressor from a given contractive one, prove improved memory, communication-complexity, and assumption requirements (including extensions to federated learning with arbitrary partial participation), and validate these theoretical gains with experiments showing better performance than EF.

The paper addresses how to build SE(3)-equivariant graph neural networks that balance expressiveness and computational efficiency for physics- and geometry-driven tasks. Its key insight is to introduce equivariant local complete frames—orthonormal bases constructed from node coordinates via cross products—that avoid direction degeneration and let tensor-valued features be projected into a compact, complete local representation. The method embeds these frames into graph neural network layers to process and combine projected tensor information efficiently (since frames are formed using only cross products), yielding an expressive yet computationally light SE(3)-equivariant architecture. Experiments on Newtonian dynamics and molecular conformation generation show the approach matches or outperforms prior equivariant models while being efficient.

result.text: The paper addresses the bias and approximation errors of random feature attentions (RFAs) that linearize softmax attention to achieve linear time and space, which can degrade fidelity compared to exact softmax. The key insight is to view RFAs as self-normalized importance samplers, which explains their bias and motivates an unbiased randomized attention (RA) estimator that uses query-specific positive random features to faithfully approximate the full softmax attention. Building on RA’s expressiveness but avoiding its quadratic cost, the authors propose Linear Randomized Attention (LARA), a novel mechanism that combines RA’s richer sampling strategy with RFA-style factorization to retain linear complexity while substantially improving approximation quality. Empirical results across domains show that RA and LARA markedly reduce approximation error and improve performance over prior RFAs.

The paper addresses federated learning under client heterogeneity in both data distributions and resource constraints, aiming to produce personalized compressed models rather than a single global model. The key insight is to combine quantized model training with knowledge distillation so that clients can collaboratively learn bespoke compressed models (with differing precisions, dimensions, and structures) by distilling shared knowledge through a global model while jointly optimizing quantization values. Methodologically, the authors formulate a relaxed optimization that treats quantization levels as variables, introduce a KD-based local objective to enable compressed personalization, and solve the resulting problem with an alternating proximal gradient algorithm whose convergence they analyze. The paper tackles catastrophic overfitting in single-step adversarial training, a sudden collapse where models become vulnerable to multi-step attacks (PGD) despite appearing robust to single-step attacks (FGSM). The key insight is that using only maximal-perturbation single-step examples concentrates training on boundary points and ignores the continuum of adversarial directions, which distorts the decision boundary and creates a highly curved loss surface that single-step updates cannot reliably defend. The authors analyze this mechanism and propose a simple remedy—augmenting or modifying single-step training to include non-maximal or diversified adversarial examples (thereby sampling the adversarial direction more broadly) to regularize curvature and preserve robustness—showing this prevents catastrophic overfitting and enables single-step procedures to resist multi-step attacks.

The paper tackles efficient, symmetry-preserving prediction of quantum Hamiltonian matrices for molecular systems, where maintaining SE(3) equivariance typically conflicts with computational and memory efficiency. On four MD17 molecular datasets QHNet matches state-of-the-art accuracy with much faster runtimes and about 50% lower memory consumption.

result.text: The paper tackles the problem of large Key-Value (KV) cache memory growth in autoregressive LLM inference, which limits long-context and high-throughput deployment. The key insight is that KV states in adjacent mid-to-deep layers are highly similar, so compressing across the depth dimension by merging layer states can greatly reduce memory without retraining. The proposed MiniCache method disentangles each KV vector into magnitude and direction, interpolates (merges) the directions of similar adjacent-layer states while preserving magnitudes, and uses a token retention strategy to skip merging for highly distinct state pairs; this training-free approach is compatible with quantization/sparsity and yields strong empirical gains (e.g., up to 5.02x compression and ~5x throughput with near-lossless quality on LLaMA-2-7B).

We propose a streaming deep active learning algorithm that optimizes a Fisher-information–based MLE error bound online by maintaining a low-rank NTK-based sketch of the empirical Fisher and selecting incoming points that maximally reduce the bound subject to a small-window diversity constraint. Concretely, we amortize BAIT-style marginal-gain computations via incremental Jacobian features and rank-r Cholesky updates, and combine them with VeSSAL’s windowed diversity to avoid redundancy at target query rates. Using the NTK embedding to analyze the linearized regime, we adapt the query threshold via regret-balancing, yielding joint guarantees on regret and label requests that recover minimax rates in the linear case. This Fisher-Stream design promises stronger label efficiency than uncertainty-only streaming while remaining scalable with O(r^2) per-candidate updates and stable online operation.

args.text: We propose Rule-Conditioned Temporal Boxes (RuCTB), a TKGC model that fuses interpretable temporal rules with time-aware box embeddings. Weighted temporal rules, extracted via temporal random-walk reasoning and equipped with interval density functions, parameterize the dilation and translation of relation–time boxes in a BoxTE-style architecture, gating how boxes expand or shift across time according to rule evidence. Training jointly optimizes box inclusion scores for timestamped triples and interval likelihoods from the rule-conditioned densities, yielding calibrated uncertainty over validity windows and robust generalization in sparse or imbalanced settings. RuCTB produces human-readable explanations via rule contributions alongside evolving box geometries and improves forecasting by aligning symbolic temporal causality with geometric validity regions.

result.text: The paper tackles the problem of generative modeling for periodic materials, where existing molecule-focused methods fail to fully account for the distinct symmetry groups and periodicity of crystal structures. The key insight is that separating the generation of discrete elements (atom types and lattice parameters) from continuous coordinates, and embedding symmetry constraints directly into the coordinate generative process, enables models that are provably invariant to material symmetries. The proposed SyMat framework uses a variational autoencoder to generate atom type sets, lattice lengths, and lattice angles, and a score-based diffusion model for atom coordinates that incorporates a novel symmetry-aware probabilistic diffusion process; together these components guarantee invariance to all symmetry transformations of periodic materials and improve performance on random generation and property-optimization benchmarks.

result.text: The paper addresses the problem of providing formal robustness guarantees for reinforcement learning policies against adversarial perturbations, both in terms of per-state action stability and worst-case cumulative reward. The key insight is that smoothing techniques applied to value-based policies can certify action invariance and lower bounds on finite-horizon returns: local smoothing around states yields protections for individual actions along a trajectory, while global smoothing (and an adaptive local search variant) can produce tight certified lower bounds on cumulative rewards. The method, called CROP, instantiates these ideas for policies derived from Q-functions by developing a local smoothing algorithm to guarantee action robustness, a global smoothing algorithm to certify finite-horizon reward bounds, and an adaptive local smoothing search to tighten reward certificates, and it empirically evaluates these certificates (and their tightness) across several robust RL training methods and four environments.

result.text: The paper addresses why adversarial training suffers from robust overfitting and its puzzling dependence on perturbation radius and data quality by identifying a previously overlooked source of error: label noise. The key insight is that adversarial perturbations distort the true label distribution of examples, so inheriting the original clean labels for adversarial counterparts introduces label noise that fuels overfitting and explains epoch-wise double descent. Methodologically, the authors analyze this label-mismatch theoretically and empirically and propose an automatic label-calibration scheme that adjusts labels for adversarial examples to counteract the noise, yielding consistent robustness improvements across models and datasets without extra hyperparameters or tuning.

args.text: I propose Counterfactually Regularized Temporal Rule Survival (CR-TRS) for event-time prediction on temporal KGs: instead of predicting a point or interval PDF alone, it models time-to-event with a rule-mixture survival model where each temporal logical rule parameterizes a hazard kernel and rule activations are gathered via differentiable random walks on a TEKG with time nodes. Training jointly learns rule weights and hazard parameters while calibrating survival curves; crucially, it augments data with causal counterfactual graph perturbations and penalizes variance of rule hazards/selection across these counterfactuals to prune spurious temporal correlations. We expect improved robustness under low-data, imbalance, or temporal shift, alongside transparent, time-localized rationales.

result.text: The paper tackles the KV-cache memory bottleneck in LLM decoding, where storing key-value pairs for all previous tokens limits deployment and existing pruning/eviction schemes hurt tasks needing long-range recall. The key insight is that adding a tiny, constant-sized recurrent cache that synthesizes and preserves summarized recurrence can complement eviction-based caches so that no token is truly unrecoverable, allowing the model to query approximate historical information without storing all KV pairs. The method, called LESS, integrates a nearly-free fixed-size recurrent cache with standard eviction or pruning strategies: during decoding LESS maintains and updates a compact summary representation of past states while evicted full KV entries remain removable, enabling the decoder to reconstruct or approximate older context when needed. Experiments show LESS substantially narrows (and sometimes closes) the performance gap with full caching across diverse tasks while drastically reducing memory use.

The paper addresses federated optimization for complex nested problems—specifically bilevel, minimax, and compositional formulations—that arise in tasks like adversarial robustness, hyperparameter tuning, and actor-critic, where standard single-level federated methods fail. The key insight is that a unified federated alternating stochastic-gradient approach with tailored hypergradient estimation and variance-reduction can handle inner–outer coupling and client heterogeneity, subsuming and adapting to bilevel, minimax, and compositional cases. The method, FedNest, alternates local stochastic updates for inner and outer variables across clients, incorporates federated hypergradient computation to propagate inner-level information, and uses variance-reduction to mitigate heterogeneity-induced bias; the authors prove convergence rates for heterogeneous data and validate the approach empirically on hyperparameter/hyper-representation learning and minimax tasks.

result.text: The paper addresses the challenge of aligning individual brains for group-level neuroimaging analysis despite large anatomical and functional variability across subjects. Its key insight is to frame inter-subject alignment as an optimal-transport problem that jointly accounts for pairwise functional relationships (Gromov–Wasserstein) and pointwise feature similarity, while allowing mass variation so cortical areas of different sizes can be matched (the “fused unbalanced” formulation). The method, Fused Unbalanced Gromov–Wasserstein (FUGW), computes a soft correspondence between cortical surfaces by minimizing a loss that combines structural relational mismatch and feature dissimilarity with an unbalanced transport penalty to permit creation/destruction of mass, producing landmark-free whole-brain alignments that penalize large topographic deformations. Empirically, FUGW yields higher between-subject correlation on independent functional data and more precise group-level functional maps than existing coarse co-registration approaches.

result.text: The paper addresses understanding and improving linearized self-attention by connecting it to Fast Weight Programmers (FWPs), i.e., systems where a slow network programs a fast memory via additive outer-product updates, and identifies capacity and adaptability limitations in recent linear attention variants. Its key insight is that linearized attention is formally equivalent to classic outer-product FWPs, which suggests replacing purely additive programming instructions with delta-rule-like updates and learned, dynamic learning rates so the fast memory can correct and adapt mappings from keys to values. result.text: The paper addresses communication bottlenecks in distributed/federated optimization by unifying two previously separate approaches for gradient compression—variance-reduced unbiased compressors (DIANA) and error-feedback for biased contractive compressors (EF21)—into a single framework that can handle both. The key insight is that compressors can be characterized by two parameters (bias and variance), and by designing an algorithm that exploits both error feedback and variance-reduction ideas one can recover DIANA and EF21 as special cases while enabling a broader class of compressors. The proposed method introduces a new algorithm (EF-BV) that operates with this generalized compressor class, combines independent randomness across workers with an error-correction mechanism, and leverages variance reduction to improve convergence as the number of workers grows. The authors prove linear convergence under suitable conditions, showing that EF-BV inherits the practical benefits of biased compressors like top-k and the theoretical scaling advantages of randomized unbiased schemes.

The key insight is that the cheap fast gradient sign method (FGSM), when paired with random input initialization and standard efficiency tricks, can produce robustness comparable to PGD-based training at a fraction of the cost, provided a specific failure mode is avoided. The authors develop and evaluate FGSM-based adversarial training protocols, demonstrate dramatic speedups (e.g., robust CIFAR-10 and ImageNet classifiers trained in minutes–hours with competitive robust accuracy), and diagnose “catastrophic overfitting” as the reason prior FGSM attempts failed, offering practical recommendations and code to reproduce their results.

args.text: I propose Rule-Constrained Temporal Counterfactual Augmentation (RTCA) for temporal KG forecasting. The method learns weighted temporal logical rules on a temporal event KG and attaches interval densities to rules, then synthesizes counterfactuals by perturbing event times and alternative relation instantiations that satisfy or minimally violate the learned rules to create balanced, drift-aware training data. A joint learner is trained on observed and counterfactual facts with a distributional consistency loss that aligns predicted time-interval densities across real and counterfactual worlds, improving robustness to data sparsity and temporal shift while retaining interpretable explanations. This yields rule-grounded counterfactual rationales for predictions and stronger generalization in forecasting and event-time prediction.

result.text: The paper addresses how to build neural networks that exactly respect symmetry under any finite-dimensional representation of a reductive Lie group, a need that arises in physics, chemistry, and geometry where data transform under groups like O(n), U(n) or the Lorentz group. The key insight is that the equivariant architectures (generalizing ACE/MACE from atomistic point clouds) can be made fully general by composing learnable maps that operate on tensors decomposed into irreducible representations and by using algebraic routines to reduce arbitrary tensor products, ensuring equivariance by construction. The method implements this idea as a modular network design plus the lie-nn software library, which automates tensor-product decomposition and projection into irreducibles so practitioners can assemble G‑equivariant layers for any reductive Lie group; the approach is validated on Lorentz-group-based top-quark tagging and orthogonal-group shape recognition tasks.

result.text: The paper tackles the mismatch between pruning objectives (minimizing remaining weights) and actual inference time, aiming to produce pruned DNNs that meet a user-specified speedup on a target system while minimizing accuracy loss. The key insight is to frame pruning as a speedup-constrained layer-wise allocation problem—optimal layer sparsities should be chosen with knowledge of both layer sensitivity and the real runtime cost on the hardware, rather than by simply reducing parameter count. SPDY implements this by combining an efficient dynamic programming solver that finds layer-wise sparsities that satisfy a desired speedup given sensitivity scores, with a local search procedure that estimates accurate per-layer sensitivity scores; the pipeline is compatible with one-shot and gradual pruning and extends to low-data and structured patterns (e.g., GPU 2:4) to empirically deliver guaranteed speedups with improved accuracy recovery.

result.text: The paper addresses the problem of training robust neural networks in federated learning (FL), where multi-step local updates and client heterogeneity create unique challenges for adversarial training and make convergence analysis difficult. The key insight is to cast federated adversarial learning (FAL) as a global min–max optimization that integrates an inner loop of adversarial example generation on each client with an outer loop of local model updates and server aggregation, and to analyze convergence by employing gradient approximation and coupling techniques tailored to the multi-local-step, non-iid setting. The method formulates a global robust training loss and proves, in the over-parameterized regime, that with appropriately chosen learning rates and sufficient communication rounds the algorithm’s minimum loss can be driven arbitrarily close to zero, despite the complications of min–max dynamics, non-gradient-aligned local updates, and inter-client heterogeneity.

The paper addresses the problem of making Bayesian Optimization (BO) robust to distributional shifts in observed contexts by framing BO as a Distributionally Robust Optimization (DRO) problem, overcoming limitations of prior work that assumed finite contexts and lacked tractable algorithms. The key insight is that robustness against a broad class of φ-divergences (which includes χ^2, total variation, and KL) admits an equivalent finite-dimensional reformulation, so the infinite-dimensional DRO-BO problem can be solved tractably even with continuous context distributions. The authors develop an algorithm based on this reformulation that is straightforward to implement, prove sublinear regret bounds for the continuous-context setting, and empirically demonstrate superior performance to existing methods, validating both practicality and theoretical guarantees.

args.text: I propose Counterfactually-Calibrated Temporal Rule Densities (C-TRuD), which couple temporal logical rules with causal counterfactual augmentation to improve robustness and interpretability in temporal KG forecasting and event-time prediction. Building on temporal rule extraction and TEKG random-walk aggregation, we associate each rule with a conditional time-interval density that is calibrated by synthetic counterfactual histories generated via a causal model over global graph structure, enforcing invariance of rule parameters to perturbations that mimic distribution shifts and sparsity. Training jointly maximizes the likelihood of observed events under the rule densities while minimizing discrepancy between factual and counterfactual rule posteriors, effectively reweighting spurious temporal correlations and sharpening rule timing. This yields stable, explainable predictions under imbalanced, few-shot, and temporally shifted regimes.

result.text: The paper addresses the challenge of generating realistic, stable periodic crystal structures, where valid materials occupy a low-dimensional manifold constrained by quantum-mechanical local energy minima and type-specific bonding preferences, and where models must respect permutation, translation, rotation, and periodic invariances. Its key insight is to combine a variational latent-space model with a diffusion-style decoder that explicitly embeds physical inductive biases: the decoder iteratively moves atomic coordinates toward lower-energy configurations while updating atom types to satisfy neighbor bonding preferences, and it models interactions across periodic boundaries. The method, called Crystal Diffusion Variational Autoencoder (CDVAE), trains on distributions of known stable materials and decodes by a learned reverse-diffusion process over positions and types that enforces invariances and periodic interactions; this yields superior performance on reconstruction, valid and diverse generation, and property optimization compared to prior approaches, alongside new datasets and evaluation metrics for the field.

We propose HARP: a post-training, hardware-aware reconstruction pruning framework that jointly selects multi-granular structured sparsity (attention heads, channels, and N:M blocks) to satisfy a user-specified latency budget on a target device while minimizing blockwise output drift. It combines a differentiable blockwise reconstruction loss with a calibrated, table-based latency surrogate and solves the constrained allocation via an augmented-Lagrangian using straight-through relaxed masks, unifying speedup-constrained layer allocation with data-driven sparsity selection. A brief per-layer reconstruction tuning step refines masks, delivering true wall-clock speedups like hardware-aware knapsack methods but with BESA-style output preservation and the runtime of fast post-training pruning. Experiments would target LLaMA and ViTs on GPUs with optional 2:4 enforcement, showing stable accuracy under strict latency budgets and mixed-granularity sparsity.

result.text: The paper addresses active learning for deep neural networks in realistic streaming scenarios where data arrive sequentially and labels must be requested on the fly rather than from an offline pool. Its key insight is that effective streaming active learning can be achieved by balancing per-sample uncertainty with diversity among a small group of recently seen points, thereby matching a target query rate without hand-tuned hyperparameters. The proposed method, VeSSAL, examines incoming data in small batches, scores candidates by a combined uncertainty-diversity objective, selects a subset to query immediately to satisfy the query budget, and updates the model incrementally; this streaming sampling scheme enables practical batch active learning for DNNs on large, fragmented, or human-in-the-loop datasets.

The moshpit mixing yields exponential convergence of matched subsets under intermittent connectivity and stragglers, eliminating masters and global sync while keeping bandwidth comparable to sparse all-to-all; empirically this should reduce duplication/oscillation and improve large-scene PSNR/LPIPS over ADMM or posterior-averaging baselines. Rare system-triggered global OT sweeps are invoked only when network mixing degrades, providing further quality gains with bounded overhead.

result.text: We propose Sketched Associative SSM: augmenting selective state-space models with a streaming, sketch-based key–value store to enable content-addressable retrieval in linear time without quadratic attention. Concretely, the model maintains compact states S1 = Σ w_i φ(k_i) and S2 = Σ w_i φ(k_i) v_i^T updated by learnable write gates; at query time it returns y ≈ (S2^T φ(q)) / (φ(q)^T S1), where φ is a high-degree polynomial feature map compressed via randomized polynomial sketching with blockwise causal masking. Using the state-space duality, these updates are implemented as additional semiseparable state transitions alongside the SSM dynamics, yielding small hardware-friendly memory while directly addressing SSM deficits in distant recall, token comparison, and the ICL retrieval gap. We expect this module to match or surpass local-attention hybrids on retrieval benchmarks (e.g., Passkey/Phonebook) and to extrapolate to 256k–1M contexts without degradation while preserving SSM-like throughput.

result.text: The paper addresses the problem of automatically designing acquisition functions (AFs) for Bayesian optimization that are robust across diverse optimization problems, avoiding ad-hoc, problem-specific choices. Its key insight is that Large Language Models (LLMs) can be leveraged as a discovery engine to synthesize novel, executable AFs from limited evaluations of representative objective functions, producing analytic and deployable expressions that generalize beyond the training set. The proposed method, FunBO, builds on FunSearch by prompting an LLM to propose candidate AFs in code, evaluating these candidates on a small set of functions to guide selection and refinement, and then validating the discovered AFs across global optimization benchmarks and hyperparameter tuning tasks. Empirically, FunBO finds AFs that often outperform standard general-purpose acquisition functions and compete with specialized, transfer-learned AFs, demonstrating strong in- and out-of-distribution generalization.

result.text: The paper addresses few-shot temporal knowledge graph reasoning: predicting future facts for newly emerging entities in evolving temporal knowledge graphs where only very limited historical observations exist and distributions may shift over time. The key insight is that rigid, one-size-fits-all neighbor sampling and aggregation fails under both data scarcity and temporal drift, so the model should learn to dynamically adapt how it selects and pools recent contextual facts for each new entity using feedback from future facts. To do this the authors propose MetaTKGR, a meta-learning framework that jointly learns temporally supervised sampling and aggregation strategies and a temporal adaptation regularizer to stabilize updates, enabling rapid, time-aware adaptation for new entities; theory and experiments on three real-world TKGs show substantial gains over static and prior meta-learning baselines.

result.text: The paper addresses the problem of performing Bayesian optimal experimental design (BOED) adaptively in real time for implicit simulation models that lack tractable likelihoods, where traditional BOED is too computationally expensive to run during experiments. The key insight is to amortize experiment-time cost by training a design policy network offline that learns to map current data and context to near-optimal next-design decisions, enabling millisecond-scale deployment without requiring closed-form likelihoods or conditional independence. The method, called implicit Deep Adaptive Design (iDAD), trains the policy on simulated differentiable samples from the model using objectives that capture expected information gain (or related utilities) and then applies the learned policy online to select experimental settings rapidly. Empirical results demonstrate that iDAD yields fast, effective adaptive designs across multiple tasks, extending policy-based BOED to a much broader class of implicit models.

The key insight is that the recently popular in-sample learning paradigm (e.g., IQL) can be understood as performing Implicit Value Regularization (IVR): by construction it regularizes value estimates implicitly so the policy improves using only actions seen in the data, avoiding OOD queries. result.text: The paper addresses why the Mamba state space model, which has linear computation complexity, performs so well on high-resolution vision tasks compared to conventional (and typically weaker) linear-attention Transformers. Its key insight is that Mamba can be reformulated as a variant of linear-attention Transformer with six systematic differences—input gate, forget gate, shortcut, no attention normalization, single-head, and a modified block design—and that among these, the forget gate and block design principally drive Mamba’s superior performance. Methodologically, the authors unify selective state space models and linear attention in a common formulation, ablate and analyze each of the six design choices through empirical studies on vision tasks, and then construct a Mamba-Inspired Linear Attention (MILA) model that integrates the critical forget gate and block-design ideas into linear attention, yielding better accuracy and faster, parallelizable inference on image classification and high-resolution dense prediction.

Curvature-guided adversarial label transport (C-GALT): We hypothesize that robust overfitting in adversarial training stems from label mismatch induced by adversarial perturbations and local nonlinearity, and propose to assign soft labels to adversarial examples by transporting the clean label distribution along the attack direction using Jacobian–vector products, with a SAM-based curvature probe to modulate transport. Concretely, we generate a one-step adversarial example (e.g., N-FGSM), estimate gradient alignment and a curvature proxy via SAM-style weight perturbations (or lightweight Hessian-norm approximations), and then interpolate the clean one-hot toward the model’s adversarial logits in proportion to misalignment/curvature, yielding per-example adaptive soft labels. This unifies adaptive label smoothing with curvature control to prevent single-step catastrophic overfitting while reducing robust overfitting from label noise, and retains efficiency by reusing quantities already available in fast training. We expect improved robustness–calibration trade-offs and more stable training across larger perturbation radii without extra hyperparameters.

result.text: We propose a compute-aware co-active learning framework that jointly selects labeled batches and a sparse parameter-update mask to maximize expected generalization gain per unit wall-clock and communication budget. Concretely, we optimize a Fisher-information–based MLE error-reduction bound restricted to a k-parameter mask (linearized/NTK regime), operationalized by alternating steps: (i) pick a fixed mask via top-k Fisher/gradient scores; (ii) choose a large, diversity-regularized batch that maximizes the restricted Fisher gain using scalable matrix sketches. This unifies Fisher-guided selection with massive-batch diversification and fixed-Fisher sparse updating, and extends naturally to streaming by maintaining a sliding-window mask and querying points whose restricted Fisher contributions cross an adaptive threshold. We hypothesize superior label efficiency under tight compute/communication budgets and propose submodular surrogates for the restricted Fisher gain to enable greedy selection with approximation guarantees.

result.text: Posterior-Consensus 3DGS (PC-3GS) is a distributed training scheme that treats each Gaussian’s parameters as a probabilistic posterior and fuses workers via uncertainty-weighted consensus rather than raw parameter averaging. Each shard runs SGLD-based updates to maintain per-parameter means/variances and communicates only low-rank sufficient statistics for Gaussians whose projected pixels cross shard boundaries; a master (or peer-to-peer ADMM) penalizes KL divergence between local and global marginals, weighting constraints by inverse variance to naturally prioritize confident updates. Partitioning and sparse all-to-all follow Grendel, while spatial blocking and ADMM-style consensus follow DOGS; MVS-guided priors initialize means/variances in texture-poor regions to stabilize early training. This yields lower bandwidth, better robustness to poor initialization, and improved quality on large scenes by aligning a product-of-experts posterior across shards.

result.text: The paper addresses loss of plasticity in continual learning—where networks become harder to train as new tasks arrive—by aiming to preserve trainability while retaining performance. args.text: We propose Partition-Aggregated Conservative Offline RL (PACORL), a poisoning-resilient offline RL method that combines in-sample conservative value learning with robust trajectory-level aggregation to provide end-to-end guarantees against a bounded fraction of poisoned trajectories. Concretely, we form a noise-seeded N-FGSM example and sample 1–2 intermediate points on the straight line x→x_adv, adding a KL loss that matches the model’s logits at each intermediate point to the linear interpolation of logits between the endpoints—acting as a cheap line-integral smoothness regularizer of the adversarial-direction curvature. This encourages locally linear behavior along adversarial directions, complements gradient-alignment intuitions, and requires only a couple extra forward passes without inner-loop attacks. I propose Rule-Calibrated Survival Dynamics (RCSD) for temporal KG time-to-event forecasting that treats each (subject, relation, object) as a survival process with an interpretable hazard over time. RCSD factorizes the hazard into a time-node base rate and multiplicative contributions from temporal logical rules compiled into nonnegative intensity kernels, aggregating path evidence on a temporal event KG to produce duration-aware predictions and support censored supervision. Rules are learned/extracted and weighted with interpretable temporal rule learners and dynamically adapted (e.g., via temporal random-walk rule induction), while a lightweight meta-learned frailty term enables rapid few-shot adaptation for newly emerging entities. Training via partial-likelihood with calibration regularizers yields calibrated event-time distributions, counterfactual reasoning by ablating rule intensities, and robust performance under sparsity and temporal drift.

result.text: This paper addresses the problem of optimizing multiple, expensive-to-evaluate objectives when design inputs are subject to random noise, causing solutions to perform worse than predicted and existing BO methods (which handle input noise) being limited to single objectives. The key insight is to formalize robustness across multiple objectives via the multivariate value-at-risk (MVaR), a risk-aware performance metric that captures worst-case quantiles of the joint objective distribution, and to approximate optimization of this intractable criterion by leveraging random scalarizations to produce tractable, informative acquisition functions. The method builds Gaussian process surrogates for the noisy, multivariate objectives, samples random scalarization weights to turn the multi-objective MVaR problem into many scalar robust subproblems, and uses these to guide Bayesian optimization in a scalable, theoretically-grounded way that empirically finds designs satisfying multiple specifications with high probability.

result.text: The paper addresses the gap between worst-case bounds and practical performance for random-projection matrix sketching used in dimensionality reduction, low-rank approximation, and randomized Newton-type optimization. Its key insight is that modern spectral random-matrix tools let one derive precise, provable expressions for the expected projection (sketch) operator—expressions that depend on the data's spectrum and capture lower-order effects and constant factors that worst-case analyses miss. The method develops novel spectral-analytic techniques to compute these expected projection matrices for common sketches (Gaussian, Rademacher, etc.), then uses those expressions to predict and analyze the performance of low-rank approximation and iterative stochastic optimization procedures in terms of the data's eigenstructure. Empirical validation shows the derived formulas closely match observed behavior across tasks and sketch types, enabling much tighter, data-dependent performance characterization.

The paper addresses Bayesian optimization for expensive black-box functions with discrete or mixed (discrete+continuous) inputs, where maximizing acquisition functions is hard because gradients are unavailable and exhaustive search is infeasible. The key insight is to replace direct optimization over discrete choices by optimizing the expectation of the acquisition function under a continuous probability distribution (probabilistic reparameterization), which lets one use gradient-based methods while preserving the original BO policy: under suitable reparameterizations the maximizer of the probabilistic objective coincides with the maximizer of the acquisition function and thus inherits the same regret guarantees. This enables inference with longer contexts and larger batches while maintaining near-MQA performance.

result.text: The paper addresses the problem of excessive KV-cache memory usage during generative inference with LLMs on long contexts, where naive eviction of key-value pairs based on attention scores degrades generation quality. The key insight is that attention importance varies both across layers (shallow vs deep) and across tokens, so a dynamic, discriminative compression strategy can selectively retain or recall KV entries to preserve salient context without fine-tuning. The proposed method, D2O, applies a two-level scheme: a layer-level dynamic allocation that adaptively protects layers with denser attention from aggressive eviction, and a token-level compensation mechanism that uses similarity thresholds to recall and merge discarded tokens with similar retained ones; this yields substantial KV-cache compression, >3× throughput improvement, and maintained long-text generation quality across benchmarks and architectures.

We propose Fed-CoBAIT-Mask, a federated compute-aware active learning framework that co-optimizes client selection, label acquisition, and a fixed top-k Fisher update mask to maximize Fisher-based MLE error reduction per transmitted bit and per compute second. Clients maintain low-rank sketches of their local empirical Fisher over a moving window and score unlabeled points by restricted Fisher gain under the mask; the server aggregates these sketches with a compression-aware SCA-style protocol and greedily schedules client/query pairs by marginal gain over communication cost. Model updates are communicated as low-rank-plus-Hadamard masked factors, while optionally training a learned sparse subnetwork to further reduce memory and uplink, yielding label-, compute-, and communication-efficient learning under heterogeneity and partial participation. We further introduce submodular surrogates for the restricted Fisher gain to enable near-optimal greedy selection, and leverage convergence guarantees from compression-aware federated optimization.

Motion-Consistent OT Consensus scales 4D Gaussian Splatting by distributing training across overlapping spatio-temporal blocks and periodically fusing them via a visibility- and motion-aware optimal transport in 4D. result.text: The paper tackles the gap between linear-attention Transformers—which offer linear-time inference and RNN-style 2D hidden-state formulations—and softmax-attention models, noting that linear attention typically lags in accuracy and existing implementations are I/O-inefficient. The key insight is that by trading off memory movement against parallelizability, one can implement a hardware-efficient linear-attention kernel that outperforms optimized softmax implementations, and that expressivity can be restored by adding data-dependent gating to the linear-attention formulation. The authors introduce FLASHLINEARATTENTION, a fast I/O-aware kernel, and extend it to Gated Linear Attention (GLA) which plugs into Transformers as a drop-in attention replacement; empirically GLA matches or exceeds LLaMA-style and other linear-time baselines on moderate-scale language modeling, generalizes remarkably to much longer contexts (training on 2K, testing >20K) with minimal perplexity loss, and trains faster than comparable linear-time models like Mamba.

The paper addresses the challenge of partial client participation in federated learning, which exacerbates data heterogeneity and causes aggregated updates to deviate from full-participation baselines. Its key insight is to split participating clients into two complementary roles—anchors that compute accurate, large-batch “bullseye” gradients and miners that perform multiple small-batch, near-optimal local updates guided by those bullseyes—so the combination compensates for missing client updates and steers the global model more reliably. The proposed method, FedAMD, implements this anchor sampling scheme by having anchor clients periodically produce high-fidelity gradient references while miner clients use those references to regularize or correct their multiple local steps before aggregation; theoretical analysis shows up to O(1/ε) fewer communication rounds to reach an ε-approximation for nonconvex objectives, and experiments confirm reduced computation/communication costs and improved test accuracy.

For each minibatch, we identify small-loss adversarial examples and spawn K diversified restarts from their locations by adding small random probes and a one-step curvature-aware push orthogonal to the current input gradient (using a GradAlign-style misalignment or a cheap hvp proxy) to steer toward high-loss, poorly aligned directions; we then train on the hardest of these variants while applying label calibration proportional to the measured misalignment to mitigate label noise. This procedure retains the coverage of strong-adversary training, converts easy cases into informative ones, and, by calibrating labels, reduces both robust and catastrophic overfitting at near single-step cost.

To preserve long-range recall, KV-ALOC fuses depth-wise adjacent-layer KV merging for redundant mid-to-deep states and maintains a tiny recurrent summary cache as a backstop for evicted tokens; dynamic attention statistics provide layer- and token-level priors to seed the optimization. This unifies speedup-constrained allocation with data-driven reconstruction for KV caches, aiming for near-lossless quality at higher compression than eviction-only or depth-only methods.

result.text: This paper addresses the problem of certifying robustness of offline reinforcement learning against training-time poisoning attacks, where an adversary can arbitrarily manipulate a subset of training trajectories. The key insight is that by defining tractable certification criteria tailored to RL—per-state action stability and cumulative reward bounds—and by using aggregation and partitioning protocols over trajectories, one can provably bound how many poisoned trajectories a learned policy can tolerate. The authors introduce COPA, a certification framework that computes these bounds, proposes temporal and other aggregation schemes to improve robustness, and analyzes the computational limits (showing some certification variants are tight while others are NP-complete). Empirical results across algorithms and environments show the proposed aggregation methods substantially boost certified robustness and that certification tightness and tolerable poisoning vary by algorithm and environment.

result.text: Line-Integrated Path Consistency for Fast Adversarial Training (LIPCon-AT): We hypothesize catastrophic overfitting stems from excessive curvature along the FGSM path and propose to explicitly supervise the continuum between clean and adversarial endpoints. Concretely, we form a noise-seeded N-FGSM example and sample 1–2 intermediate points on the straight line x→x_adv, adding a KL loss that matches the model’s logits at each intermediate point to the linear interpolation of logits between the endpoints—acting as a cheap line-integral smoothness regularizer of the adversarial-direction curvature. This encourages locally linear behavior along adversarial directions, complements gradient-alignment intuitions, and requires only a couple extra forward passes without inner-loop attacks. We expect LIPCon-AT to prevent catastrophic overfitting at larger radii and to improve robustness–calibration trade-offs over standard single-step training.

result.text: The paper tackles the scalability bottleneck of 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) training, which is typically restricted to a single GPU and thus cannot handle high-resolution or large-scale scenes; the key insight is that because each Gaussian only contributes to a small, dynamic subset of pixels, training can be distributed by communicating only the required Gaussians to the corresponding pixel partitions and dynamically balancing load. They implement this idea in Grendel, a distributed system that partitions 3DGS parameters across GPUs, uses sparse all-to-all communication to transfer relevant Gaussians to pixel shards, supports batched multi-view training (rather than one view at a time), and applies a simple sqrt(batch size) hyperparameter scaling rule. By enabling dynamic partitioning and sparse communication, Grendel scales 3DGS to tens of millions of Gaussians across many GPUs and demonstrably improves reconstruction quality on large, high-resolution scenes (e.g., raising PSNR from 26.28 to 27.28 on Rubble by moving from 11.2M Gaussians on one GPU to 40.4M on 16 GPUs).

result.text: The paper addresses the dual challenges in federated learning of high communication overhead from frequent server–client synchronization and the limited adaptivity of SGD-based updates, noting that existing approaches (compression or adaptive optimizers) do not jointly resolve both issues. The key insight is that communication-efficient compression can be integrated with adaptive optimization in a principled way that preserves convergence guarantees: by designing compressors and adaptive update rules that control the additional variance and bias introduced by compression, one can retain the same nonconvex stochastic convergence rate as uncompressed adaptive methods. The method, FedCAMS, combines momentum/second-moment style adaptive updates with tailored communication compression and server–client aggregation rules, and the authors prove FedCAMS achieves O(1/√(T K m)) convergence in the nonconvex setting while validating its empirical performance across benchmarks.

result.text: The paper addresses the problem of robust overfitting in adversarial training, where models trained with strong adversaries lose robustness after prolonged training and the causes remain unclear. The key insight is that weak adversaries generate mostly small-loss adversarial examples while strong adversaries produce a diverse mix including many large-loss examples, and that some small-loss examples in strong-adversary training are “unworthy” and drive overfitting by being overly easy to fit. To mitigate this, the authors propose Minimum Loss Constrained Adversarial Training (MLCAT), which in each minibatch continues to train on large-loss examples but deliberately prevents overfitting to small-loss examples by increasing their loss (hindering their fitting), with two practical algorithmic implementations. Experiments show MLCAT eliminates robust overfitting and improves adversarial robustness across settings.

result.text: Curvature-Guided Adversarial Recycling (CGAR): We posit that robust overfitting under strong attacks arises when training repeatedly reinforces “unworthy” small-loss adversarial examples; instead of hindering them or discarding them, we recycle them into harder variants. For each minibatch, we identify small-loss adversarial examples and spawn K diversified restarts from their locations by adding small random probes and a one-step curvature-aware push orthogonal to the current input gradient (using a GradAlign-style misalignment or a cheap hvp proxy) to steer toward high-loss, poorly aligned directions; we then train on the hardest of these variants while applying label calibration proportional to the measured misalignment to mitigate label noise. Large-loss adversarial examples are kept unchanged. This procedure retains the coverage of strong-adversary training, converts easy cases into informative ones, and, by calibrating labels, reduces both robust and catastrophic overfitting at near single-step cost.

result.text: The paper addresses the problem of learning probability distributions defined on manifolds while respecting the intrinsic symmetries (group actions) those manifolds admit, a requirement common in scientific domains like physics but often ignored by existing models. Its key insight is that one can build invertible generative maps (flows) on manifolds that are equivariant with respect to the relevant symmetry group, which ensures the induced densities are symmetry-invariant and that the flow structure is compatible with manifold geometry. Methodologically, the authors develop the theoretical foundations for equivariant manifold flows—constructing equivariant diffeomorphisms and change-of-variable formulas tailored to arbitrary manifolds and group actions—and demonstrate the approach by training gauge-invariant flows to model densities over SU(n) for quantum field theory tasks.

result.text: FetchSGD addresses the dual challenges in federated learning of heavy communication costs and degraded convergence when client participation is sparse. The key insight is to use a linear, mergeable Count Sketch to compress client model updates so that momentum and error accumulation can be maintained centrally inside the sketch rather than on each client, which preserves state across intermittent clients and enables high compression without losing critical optimization history. result.text: The paper addresses the diversity and limitations of associative memory models (e.g., classical Hopfield nets, SDMs, modern continuous Hopfield nets) by asking how they can be unified and improved, particularly regarding similarity measures and memory capacity. Its key insight is that these models can all be seen as a three-step process—similarity, separation, and projection—and that varying the similarity and separation functions within this framework yields different associative memories with provable energy dynamics. The authors formalize this unified framework by extending Krotov & Hopfield (2020) to derive neural-network dynamics with local computation and a general Lyapunov energy function that guarantees convergence, and they instantiate many existing models as special cases. Empirically, they show that replacing the usual dot-product similarity with distance-based measures (e.g., Euclidean or Manhattan) markedly improves retrieval robustness and increases memory capacity across several tasks.

The key insight is to define a mutual information (MI) that explicitly incorporates uncertainty about feasibility and to use a provably non-negative lower bound on that MI, avoiding the negative acquisition values that can occur with naive constrained extensions of max-value entropy search (MES). Methodologically, the authors derive a Monte Carlo estimator of this MI lower bound (CMES-IBO), prove its low-variance properties, and extend the framework to parallel (batch) selection via conditional MI, then validate the approach on benchmarks and real-world tasks.

The paper addresses computing Wasserstein (Bures) barycenters of Gaussian distributions, where the objective on the manifold of positive-definite covariances is geodesically nonconvex and prior convergence guarantees for Riemannian gradient descent (RGD) scaled poorly with dimension. The key insight is that stronger, problem-specific geodesic convexity properties hold for the Gaussian barycenter (and related entropic-regularized barycenters and geometric median) which tightly control iterates and prevent the pathological behaviors that produce exponential dimension dependence. Building on these curvature and control estimates, the authors analyze RGD to prove dimension-free convergence rates and extend the same techniques to give the first RGD guarantees for entropically-regularized barycenters and the geometric median on the Bures–Wasserstein manifold.

The paper addresses offline constrained reinforcement learning, where a policy must be learned from fixed data to maximize return while provably satisfying safety/cost constraints despite off-policy evaluation errors. The key insight is to perform optimization in the stationary distribution space and to directly estimate stationary distribution corrections for the optimal policy with respect to returns, enabling conservative control over cost estimates rather than relying on error-prone value-based off-policy evaluation. The proposed method, COptiDICE, formulates a constrained optimization that estimates these distribution corrections from the dataset and enforces an upper bound on expected costs to produce a cost-conservative policy; empirical results show it better balances return maximization and constraint satisfaction compared to baselines.

The paper tackles the quadratic time and memory bottleneck of self-attention in Transformers for long-context language modeling by replacing softmax attention with a scalable alternative. The key insight is that high-degree polynomial attention can match softmax’s modeling power while admitting efficient linear-time computation via randomized polynomial sketching from numerical linear algebra, avoiding attention sparsification and providing provable approximation guarantees. Methodologically, the authors develop sketching techniques to compress polynomial feature maps, a block-based algorithm to enforce causal masking, and integrate these into PolySketchFormer—a practical Transformer that implements linear-time polynomial attention with theoretical bounds—and validate it on synthetic and real datasets (PG19, Wikipedia, C4), demonstrating 2.5–4× training speedups at 32k context lengths versus FlashAttention without quality loss.

result.text: The paper tackles machine unlearning (MU), aiming to remove the influence of specified data, classes, or concepts from trained models—an increasingly urgent need under data regulations—while addressing shortcomings in unlearning accuracy, stability, and applicability across domains. Its key insight is to define and exploit "weight saliency," analogous to input saliency in explanations, to focus unlearning updates on the most influential model weights rather than indiscriminately altering the entire parameter set. The proposed method, SalUn, computes gradient-based weight saliency to identify and selectively modify high-saliency weights to erase the target information, yielding an efficient, stable procedure that closely matches exact unlearning (retraining from scratch) and generalizes to both image classification and generative diffusion models. Empirically, SalUn narrows the performance gap to exact unlearning (e.g., a 0.2% gap on CIFAR-10) and attains near-100% unlearning of harmful concepts in conditional diffusion models, outperforming prior baselines.

The paper tackles catastrophic overfitting in single-step adversarial training, a sudden collapse where models become vulnerable to multi-step attacks (PGD) despite appearing robust to single-step attacks (FGSM). The key insight is that using only maximal-perturbation single-step examples concentrates training on boundary points and ignores the continuum of adversarial directions, which distorts the decision boundary and creates a highly curved loss surface that single-step updates cannot reliably defend. The authors analyze this mechanism and propose a simple remedy—augmenting or modifying single-step training to include non-maximal or diversified adversarial examples (thereby sampling the adversarial direction more broadly) to regularize curvature and preserve robustness—showing this prevents catastrophic overfitting and enables single-step procedures to resist multi-step attacks.

The key insight is that input-dependent variance functions generally face a curse of dimensionality that forces them to have low semi-elasticity, undermining formal certification guarantees unless strong restrictions are imposed. Mask-Aware Active Learning aligns sample selection with constrained training by optimizing a Fisher-information bound computed on a sparse, fixed update mask. We alternate between (infrequent) mask updates that select top-k parameters by Fisher score and (frequent) batch selection that scores candidates by their incremental reduction of the masked Fisher-based MLE error bound, while adding a lightweight diversification step to avoid redundancy. This prioritizes examples whose gradients concentrate on the updatable parameters, yielding strong label efficiency under tight compute/communication budgets (e.g., federated or on-device training). The approach preserves BAIT’s theory-driven selection while integrating fixed-Fisher-mask training and scalable diversification to remain practical at large scale.

result.text: The paper addresses how to build neural networks that universally approximate functions obeying the common symmetries of classical physics (translations, rotations, reflections/parity, boosts and permutations) across Euclidean, Lorentz, and Poincaré groups in any dimension. Its key insight is that any nonlinear equivariant map for these groups can be expressed using a compact set of scalar invariants—scalar products and scalar contractions formed from scalar, vector, and tensor inputs—so high-order irreps or heavy tensor machinery are not necessary. Methodologically, the authors prove universal approximation results by constructing polynomial equivariants from these scalar building blocks and demonstrate in experiments that architectures built around these scalar features are simple, efficient, and scalable compared with more complicated equivariant frameworks.

The paper tackles the problem of large Key-Value (KV) cache memory growth in autoregressive LLM inference, which limits long-context and high-throughput deployment. The key insight is that KV states in adjacent mid-to-deep layers are highly similar, so compressing across the depth dimension by merging layer states can greatly reduce memory without retraining. The proposed MiniCache method disentangles each KV vector into magnitude and direction, interpolates (merges) the directions of similar adjacent-layer states while preserving magnitudes, and uses a token retention strategy to skip merging for highly distinct state pairs; this training-free approach is compatible with quantization/sparsity and yields strong empirical gains (e.g., up to 5.02x compression and ~5x throughput with near-lossless quality on LLaMA-2-7B).

Its key insight is that the classical stochastic controlled averaging (SCA) can be reformulated into an equivalent but simpler and more communication-efficient implementation that halves uplink cost and serves as a foundation for compression-aware algorithms. Methodologically, the authors propose a "prune first, then unlearn" paradigm plus a sparsity-aware unlearning algorithm that incorporates sparsity regularization into training and unlearning steps, and they validate the approach theoretically and empirically, showing large gains (e.g., 77% improvement for fine-tuning) across unlearning tasks as well as benefits for backdoor defense and transfer learning.

The paper addresses temporal knowledge graph completion, focusing on the challenge of predicting time-sensitive events while capturing both timeliness and causality—properties that prior methods struggle to represent simultaneously. The key insight is to combine temporal logic-derived causal rules with time-independent commonsense knowledge so that embeddings encode event causality and general plausibility separately but jointly inform predictions. Methodologically, LCGE learns time-sensitive embeddings regularized by a temporal rule-learning algorithm that extracts and enforces causal predicate relationships, and integrates auxiliary commonsense embeddings to evaluate event plausibility, yielding improved prediction accuracy and causal explainability on TKGC benchmarks.

result.text: The paper tackles efficient, symmetry-preserving prediction of quantum Hamiltonian matrices for molecular systems, where maintaining SE(3) equivariance typically conflicts with computational and memory efficiency. The key insight is an architectural design that enforces SE(3)-equivariance while drastically reducing costly tensor-product operations and preventing exponential channel growth as atom types increase. The authors propose QHNet, an SE(3)-equivariant graph neural network that restructures equivariant message passing to cut tensor products by 92%, streamlines channels to limit dimensional blowup, and uses this lightweight equivariant circuitry to predict Hamiltonian entries. On four MD17 molecular datasets QHNet matches state-of-the-art accuracy with much faster runtimes and about 50% lower memory consumption.

result.text: The paper addresses the bias and approximation errors of random feature attentions (RFAs) that linearize softmax attention to achieve linear time and space, which can degrade fidelity compared to exact softmax. The key insight is to view RFAs as self-normalized importance samplers, which explains their bias and motivates an unbiased randomized attention (RA) estimator that uses query-specific positive random features to faithfully approximate the full softmax attention. Building on RA’s expressiveness but avoiding its quadratic cost, the authors propose Linear Randomized Attention (LARA), a novel mechanism that combines RA’s richer sampling strategy with RFA-style factorization to retain linear complexity while substantially improving approximation quality. Empirical results across domains show that RA and LARA markedly reduce approximation error and improve performance over prior RFAs.

result.text: The paper addresses the problem of machine unlearning for Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs), specifically how to make a model forget the visual recognition of a leaked or sensitive concept while preserving overall utility. The key insight is that effective unlearning can be achieved by minimally fine-tuning the model with a single representative image per concept if the fine-tuning data are multifaceted and the loss encourages synchronized forgetting and retention. The proposed Single Image Unlearning (SIU) method builds four targeted fine-tuning examples per concept and trains with a joint objective combining a novel Dual Masked KL-divergence loss (to steer the model away from recognizing the concept while protecting other behaviors) and cross-entropy (to maintain task performance), achieving strong deletion on the new MMUBench benchmark and additionally mitigating membership-inference and jailbreak attacks.

The paper addresses why adversarial training suffers from robust overfitting and its puzzling dependence on perturbation radius and data quality by identifying a previously overlooked source of error: label noise. The key insight is that adversarial perturbations distort the true label distribution of examples, so inheriting the original clean labels for adversarial counterparts introduces label noise that fuels overfitting and explains epoch-wise double descent. Methodologically, the authors analyze this label-mismatch theoretically and empirically and propose an automatic label-calibration scheme that adjusts labels for adversarial examples to counteract the noise, yielding consistent robustness improvements across models and datasets without extra hyperparameters or tuning.

result.text: The paper addresses the problem of predicting event times in temporal knowledge graphs (TKGs), where embedding-based ranking approaches struggle to capture temporal order and distance relationships and to provide interpretable, robust predictions under limited or imbalanced data. The key insight is to convert a TKG into a temporal event knowledge graph (TEKG) that explicitly represents time as nodes, enabling logical reasoning over temporal structure and the use of probabilistic rules tied to query intervals. The method implements a differentiable random walk on the TEKG to aggregate evidence from temporal and relational paths, and associates logical rules with conditional probability density functions over intervals to produce interval-based time predictions and explanations. Empirically, TEILP outperforms state-of-the-art baselines across five benchmarks and shows improved robustness in low-data, imbalanced, and forecasting-only scenarios while offering interpretable rule-based justifications.

result.text: The paper addresses the problem of building neural networks that are equivariant to orthogonal and Euclidean transformations in any dimension by leveraging algebraic structure rather than designing separate architectures per dimension. Its key insight is to use the Clifford group—an orthogonal-automorphism subgroup of the Clifford algebra that preserves multivector grading and the geometric (multiplicative) structure—so that the group action decomposes into non-equivalent subrepresentations matching multivector grades and thus yields rich, structured equivariant feature spaces. Methodologically, the authors construct neural layers whose linear and nonlinear maps are constrained by Clifford-group equivariance, show that polynomial and multiplicative operations on multivectors remain equivariant, and implement a single core model that generalizes across inner-product spaces of arbitrary dimension; empirically this approach achieves state-of-the-art results on diverse tasks including 3D n-body, 4D Lorentz-equivariant high-energy physics, and a 5D convex hull problem.

args.text: We propose Fisher-Subspace Broadcast Active FL (FiSBA): the server maintains a mergeable sketch of the global empirical Fisher, extracts a top-r eigenspace, and downlink-broadcasts a seed-coded orthonormal basis so one-shot clients can both score unlabeled samples by subspace Fisher gain (for BAIT-style query selection) and return only low-dimensional coefficients for updates. We provide a subspace-capture analysis showing near-optimal MLE-error reduction when the Fisher spectrum is concentrated and use a submodular surrogate for greedy selection in the broadcast basis. Concretely, we meta-search analytic AF templates à la FunBO that combine standard utilities (EI/UCB) with entropy and geometry-correction terms, then optimize the AF’s expectation under a reparameterized latent distribution with straight-through rounding and a trust-region, as in latent BO with probabilistic objectives. The geometry term is estimated via local linearization of the decoder or finite-difference rounding stability and calibrated to preserve regret under Lipschitz decoders, yielding AFs that better align latent search with discrete candidates. ECE-Guided Adversarial Calibration (EGAC): We hypothesize that robust and catastrophic overfitting in fast adversarial training are exacerbated by overconfident predictions on adversarial inputs and by label mismatch, so directly optimizing calibration on adversarial batches can regularize training. result.text: The paper addresses the high memory and compute cost of storing KV caches during LLM inference, noting that prior post-training compression methods ignore redundancy across the hidden (feature) dimension of KV tensors. The key insight is that KV tensors are often low-rank along the hidden dimension, so one can compress cached keys and values via low-rank projections and reconstruct them on the fly to save memory with minimal accuracy loss. The method, called Palu, decomposes linear layers into medium-grained low-rank factors, searches for efficient per-layer ranks, integrates low-rank-aware quantization, and implements fused GPU kernels to cache compressed intermediate states and reconstruct full keys/values during attention; experiments show about 50% KV-cache reduction and substantial inference speedups (up to ~1.9–2.9x with quantization) while preserving or even improving perplexity versus quantization-only baselines.

args.text: We propose Compress-BAIT, an active learner that optimizes a BAIT-style Fisher MLE-error bound explicitly under uplink/downlink compression by incorporating compressor-induced gradient covariance and bias into a compressed Fisher objective and penalty. Clients maintain low-rank sketches of Jacobian features alongside compressor noise statistics, and the server scores client/query pairs by marginal reduction in the compressed-bound per transmitted bit while jointly choosing compressor settings (e.g., quantization level). To control bias and variance in practice, the server broadcasts tiny residual seeds to induce near-unbiased uplink aggregation and uses a DoCoFL-compatible downlink scheme, yielding acquisition decisions that remain faithful under heavy bi-directional compression. We provide submodular surrogates and show the objective reduces to a scaled BAIT under SCALLION-style unbiased compression, while SCAFCOM-style biased compression with error feedback keeps the bias term bounded, preserving greedy selection guarantees.

Shards asynchronously exchange only overlapping blocks, solve tiny OT problems to obtain soft correspondences, and push/average sufficient statistics (means, covariances, SH) with uncertainty/opacity weights, while spawning/pruning unmatched mass locally to avoid brittle parameter equality. The moshpit mixing yields exponential convergence of matched subsets under intermittent connectivity and stragglers, eliminating masters and global sync while keeping bandwidth comparable to sparse all-to-all; empirically this should reduce duplication/oscillation and improve large-scene PSNR/LPIPS over ADMM or posterior-averaging baselines. Rare system-triggered global OT sweeps are invoked only when network mixing degrades, providing further quality gains with bounded overhead.

result.text: The paper addresses offline reinforcement learning in partially observable Markov decision processes (POMDPs) when the offline dataset is confounded by latent states that influence both actions and observations, a setting that breaks standard offline RL methods. The key insight is to combine pessimism for distributional shift with proximal causal inference using proxy variables to correct confounding, constructing coupled pessimistic confidence regions that account for both partial observability and unobserved confounders. The proposed P3O algorithm implements this by casting proximal causal correction as a minimax estimation problem and building a sequence of pessimistic value-function estimates under general function approximation; under a partial coverage assumption on the dataset it is shown to obtain n^{-1/2}-suboptimality with n trajectories, yielding the first provably efficient offline RL method for confounded POMDPs.

The paper addresses improving learning-based sketching methods (like CountSketch) for compressing data before fast optimization—pointing out that prior work only learned the nonzero values of sparse sketch matrices while keeping their positions fixed. The key insight is that jointly learning the positions of nonzeros as well as their values can substantially reduce sketching error, but doing so requires new algorithms that balance accuracy and training speed. The authors propose a greedy position-selection algorithm and faster alternatives tailored to low-rank approximation and Hessian approximation for second-order constrained optimization (e.g., LASSO, nuclear-norm problems), showing empirically that these methods yield significantly lower error and practical training times even with limited training data.

The paper addresses the problem of evaluating machine unlearning (MU) in diffusion models, where current benchmarks are incomplete or inaccurate for assessing removal of undesirable artistic styles and object concepts. The key insight is that a high-resolution, stylized image dataset specifically designed to capture diverse artistic styles and associated objects, combined with a standardized automated evaluation framework, enables more accurate, granular, and reproducible assessment of unlearning performance. The authors present UnlearnCanvas, a curated dataset and a suite of seven quantitative metrics, and use them to benchmark nine state-of-the-art MU methods across standard and adversarial scenarios (including fine-grained and sequential unlearning), revealing each method’s strengths, weaknesses, and failure modes. By releasing the dataset, benchmarks, and code, they provide a platform to drive development of more effective and robust unlearning techniques for safer diffusion model deployment.

Its key insight is to introduce equivariant local complete frames—orthonormal bases constructed from node coordinates via cross products—that avoid direction degeneration and let tensor-valued features be projected into a compact, complete local representation. The method embeds these frames into graph neural network layers to process and combine projected tensor information efficiently (since frames are formed using only cross products), yielding an expressive yet computationally light SE(3)-equivariant architecture. Experiments on Newtonian dynamics and molecular conformation generation show the approach matches or outperforms prior equivariant models while being efficient.

result.text: The paper addresses building a practical, high-performance NLP system for detecting diverse undesired content in real-world moderation settings. Its key insight is that robust moderation requires an end-to-end, data- and process-centric pipeline—careful taxonomy and label design, strict annotation quality controls, targeted active learning to surface rare but critical examples, and modeling techniques that prioritize generalization over narrow fits—rather than relying solely on model architecture. The authors implement this by constructing comprehensive taxonomies and clear instructions, instituting rigorous annotation and quality checks, using active learning to iteratively sample difficult/rare cases, and applying robustness and regularization strategies during training to produce classifiers that cover sexual content, hate, violence, self-harm, and harassment and that outperform generic off-the-shelf models.

args.text: We propose Certifiably Safe Conservative Offline RL (CS2-ORL), which integrates stationary-distribution constrained offline RL with randomized-smoothing-based observation robustness and in-sample conservative value learning. We learn smoothed reward and cost estimators around dataset states and compute per-state certified return lower bounds and cost upper bounds; these calibrate Lagrange multipliers and a CQL-style penalty while restricting policy improvement to in-dataset actions in proportion to the certified radius. Updates become monotone in a certificate that guarantees constraint satisfaction under L2-bounded observation perturbations up to a target radius, and we use a restricted input-dependent smoothing design to preserve formal certification validity. We expect stronger safe returns and end-to-end certificates than COptiDICE-, CQL-, or RORL-style baselines on perturbed D4RL-Safety tasks without online interaction.

result.text: The paper addresses the dual problems of adversarial vulnerability and miscalibration in neural networks by investigating their relationship and using this connection to improve trustworthiness of model predictions. The key insight is that inputs which are easily attacked (low adversarial robustness) are more likely to be poorly calibrated, so selectively softening labels for those examples can reduce overconfidence and improve calibration. The authors propose Adversarial Robustness based Adaptive Label Smoothing (AR-AdaLS), which measures how easily each training example can be adversarially perturbed and adaptively smooths its label accordingly during training; this approach improves calibration on in-distribution and shifted data and can be applied to ensembles for further gains.
